cards.title: Exercise 1 — WINDOW FUNCTIONS — Ranking
cards.prompt:
For each category, rank customers by total spending.
Show: category, customer_id, total_spent, rank within category
Only include completed transactions with non-null amounts
cards.answer:
with customer_category_totals as (
    select category, customer_id, sum(amount) as total_spent
    from transactions
    where status = 'completed' and amount is not null
    group by category, customer_id
)
select category, customer_id, total_spent,
rank() over(partition by category order by total_spent desc) as category_rank
from customer_category_totals
order by category, category_rank;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 2 — WINDOW FUNCTIONS — LAG/LEAD
cards.prompt:
For each customer, show each completed transaction with:
- previous transaction amount
- difference from previous transaction
- running total of all their transactions
Order by customer_id, transaction_date
cards.answer:
with c_tr as (
    select customer_id, transaction_date, amount
    from transactions
    where status = 'completed' and amount is not null
    order by customer_id, transaction_date
)
select customer_id, transaction_date, amount,
lag(amount) over(partition by customer_id order by transaction_date) as prev_amount,
amount - lag(amount) over(partition by customer_id order by transaction_date) as diff_from_prev,
sum(amount) over(partition by customer_id order by transaction_date) as running_total
from c_tr;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 3 — DEDUPLICATION
cards.prompt:
Find and remove duplicate transactions.
Duplicates = same customer_id, same amount, same transaction_date
Keep only the EARLIEST record (lowest updated_at)
Show the deduplicated result set
cards.answer:
-- postgres
select distinct on (customer_id, amount, transaction_date) *
from transactions
order by customer_id, amount, transaction_date, updated_at asc;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 4 — CTE + AGGREGATION
cards.prompt:
Using CTEs, calculate:
1. Each customer's total spending (completed only, non-null amounts)
2. The overall average customer spending
3. Classify each customer as 'above_average' or 'below_average'
4. Show: customer_id, name, total_spent, avg_spending, classification
cards.answer:
with tmp_view as (
	select c.customer_id, c.name
	, sum(t.amount) as total_spent
	, round(avg(t.amount),2) as avg_spending
	from customers c
	join transactions t on c.customer_id = t.customer_id
	where t.status = 'completed' and t.amount is not null
	group by c.customer_id, c.name
	order by transaction_date desc
)
select customer_id, name, total_spent, avg_spending
, case when total_spent > avg_spending
then 'above_average'
when total_spent < avg_spending
then 'below_average'
when total_spent = avg_spending
then 'equal'
else 'checking' end as classification
from tmp_view;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 5 — CHURN DETECTION
cards.prompt:
Find customers who:
a) Have NOT made any transaction in the last 60 days
   (use '2024-07-15' as "today")
b) OR have never made a transaction
Show: customer_id, name, last_transaction_date, days_since_last_tx
Order by days_since_last_tx DESC (most churned first)
cards.answer:
-- postgres
select c.customer_id, c.name, max(t.transaction_date) as last_transaction_date,
case
when max(t.transaction_date) is null then 9999
else date '2024-07-15' - max(t.transaction_date) end as days_since_last_tx
from customers c
left join transactions t on c.customer_id = t.customer_id
group by c.customer_id, c.name
having max(t.transaction_date) < date '2024-07-15' - interval '60 days'
or max(t.transaction_date) is null
order by days_since_last_tx desc;

-- never did transaction
SELECT 
    c.customer_id, 
    c.name, 
    MAX(t.transaction_date) AS last_transaction_date,
    -- Agora deixamos NULL para quem nunca comprou
    DATE '2024-07-15' - MAX(t.transaction_date) AS days_since_last_tx
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING MAX(t.transaction_date) < DATE '2024-07-15' - INTERVAL '60 days'
   OR MAX(t.transaction_date) IS NULL
-- Força os clientes que nunca compraram (NULL) a aparecerem primeiro!
ORDER BY days_since_last_tx DESC NULLS FIRST;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 6 — MONTH-OVER-MONTH GROWTH
cards.prompt:
Calculate month-over-month revenue growth:
- Monthly revenue (completed transactions only, non-null amounts)
- Previous month revenue (using LAG)
- Growth percentage
- Cumulative revenue (running total across months)
Show: month, revenue, prev_month_revenue, growth_pct, cumulative_revenue
cards.answer:
-- postgres
with monthly_revenue as (
    select date_trunc('month', transaction_date) as month,
    sum(amount) as revenue
    from transactions
    where status = 'completed' and amount is not null
    group by date_trunc('month', transaction_date)
)
select month, revenue,
lag(revenue) over(order by month) as prev_month_revenue,
round((revenue - lag(revenue) over(order by month)) / lag(revenue) over(order by month) * 100, 2) as growth_pct,
sum(revenue) over(order by month) as cumulative_revenue
from monthly_revenue
order by month;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 7 — TOP N PER GROUP
cards.prompt:
Find the top 2 highest-spending customers per city.
Use completed transactions only.
Show: city, customer_id, name, total_spent, city_rank
cards.answer:
-- postgres
with customer_city_spending as (
    select c.city, c.customer_id, c.name, sum(t.amount) as total_spent,
    rank() over(partition by c.city order by sum(t.amount) desc) as city_rank
    from customers c
    join transactions t on c.customer_id = t.customer_id
    where t.status = 'completed' and t.amount is not null
    group by c.city, c.customer_id, c.name
)
select city, customer_id, name, total_spent, city_rank
from customer_city_spending
where city_rank <= 2
order by city, city_rank;

-- ============================================================

O método .split("@") divide a string em duas partes usando o @ como separador:

O índice [1] pega o que vem depois do @ (o domínio).

No seu exemplo:

Sim, a solução faz todo o sentido e está muito bem pensada!

Aquele 9999 ali é um "truque" (uma convenção) usado por causa do requisito de ordenação do exercício: Order by days_since_last_tx DESC (most churned first) (mostrar quem está há mais tempo sem comprar primeiro).

Vou te explicar exatamente o porquê dele existir e como ele resolve o problema.

Por que usar o 9999?
O exercício pede para incluir clientes que nunca fizeram uma transação (item B). Se o cliente nunca comprou, o max(t.transaction_date) dele será NULL.

Se você tentar calcular a diferença de dias de uma data com NULL, o resultado em days_since_last_tx também será NULL.

Aí entra o problema da ordenação (ORDER BY DESC):

No PostgreSQL, por padrão, os valores NULL são considerados "maiores" que qualquer número e aparecem no topo do ORDER BY DESC.

Em outros bancos de dados, o NULL pode ser considerado o "menor" valor e aparecer no fim.

Para não depender do comportamento padrão do banco e garantir que quem nunca comprou seja considerado o "nível máximo de churn" (afinal, eles estão há "infinitos" dias sem comprar), o autor do código substituiu o NULL por um número artificialmente muito alto: 9999.

Assim, no ORDER BY days_since_last_tx DESC, quem tem 9999 dias vai ficar obrigatoriamente no topo da lista, seguido por quem comprou há 100 dias, 61 dias, etc.

Uma alternativa mais elegante (padrão SQL)
Em vez de "chutar" um número como 9999, o PostgreSQL possui uma cláusula nativa para controlar onde os NULLs devem aparecer na ordenação: NULLS FIRST ou NULLS LAST.

Se você quisesse deixar o código mais limpo sem precisar do 9999, poderia fazer assim:

SQL
SELECT 
    c.customer_id, 
    c.name, 
    MAX(t.transaction_date) AS last_transaction_date,
    -- Agora deixamos NULL para quem nunca comprou
    DATE '2024-07-15' - MAX(t.transaction_date) AS days_since_last_tx
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING MAX(t.transaction_date) < DATE '2024-07-15' - INTERVAL '60 days'
   OR MAX(t.transaction_date) IS NULL
-- Força os clientes que nunca compraram (NULL) a aparecerem primeiro!
ORDER BY days_since_last_tx DESC NULLS FIRST; 
Um detalhe sobre o seu script
Reparei que no final do arquivo há duas queries (a principal e uma escrita embaixo -- never did transaction). A primeira query (com o LEFT JOIN e o HAVING) já resolve todo o exercício sozinha, pois ela traz tanto quem está há 60 dias sem comprar quanto quem nunca comprou. A segunda query isolada não é necessária para o resultado final.

cards.title: Exercise 8 — DATA QUALITY REPORT
cards.prompt:
Create a data quality report for the transactions table showing:

- total_records

- null_customer_count

- null_amount_count

- duplicate_count (same customer_id + amount + date)

- orphan_count (customer_id not in customers table, excluding nulls)

- refunded_pct (percentage of refunded transactions)

All in ONE query (one row result)
cards.answer:
-- postgres
WITH duplicate_metrics AS (
    -- Isolamos o cálculo de duplicados em um bloco separado e legível
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS duplicate_groups
    FROM (
        SELECT customer_id, amount, transaction_date
        FROM transactions
        WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
        GROUP BY customer_id, amount, transaction_date
        HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
    ) dups
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_records,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t.customer_id IS NULL) AS null_customer_count,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t.amount IS NULL) AS null_amount_count,
    -- Buscamos o valor calculado na CTE lá em cima
    (SELECT duplicate_groups FROM duplicate_metrics) AS duplicate_groups,
    -- Uma forma mais limpa (usando NOT EXISTS) para os órfãos
    COUNT(*) FILTER (
        WHERE t.customer_id IS NOT NULL 
          AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = t.customer_id)
    ) AS orphan_count,
    ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t.status = 'refunded')::DECIMAL / COUNT(*) * 100, 2) AS refunded_pct
FROM transactions t;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 9 — COMPLEX JOIN + ANALYTICS
cards.prompt:
For each product category, calculate:
- total_revenue (from order_items)
- unique_customers
- avg_order_value
- best_selling_product (name of product with highest quantity sold)
- pct_of_total_revenue (this category's % of all revenue)
cards.answer:
-- postgres
WITH category_revenue AS (
    SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS unique_customers,
    AVG(o.total_amount) AS avg_order_value
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
),
best_products AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.category) p.category, p.name AS best_selling_product
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category, p.name
    ORDER BY p.category, SUM(oi.quantity) DESC
),
grand_total AS (
    SELECT SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items
)
SELECT cr.category, cr.total_revenue, cr.unique_customers, ROUND(cr.avg_order_value, 2) AS avg_order_value,
bp.best_selling_product,
ROUND(cr.total_revenue / gt.total * 100, 2) AS pct_of_total_revenue
FROM category_revenue cr
JOIN best_products bp ON cr.category = bp.category
CROSS JOIN grand_total gt
ORDER BY cr.total_revenue DESC;

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 10 — SESSIONIZATION (HARD — common in interviews)
cards.prompt:
Group customer transactions into "sessions":
A new session starts when there's a gap of > 30 days between
consecutive transactions for the same customer.
Show: customer_id, transaction_id, transaction_date, session_number

Hint: use LAG to find gaps, then SUM to create session IDs
cards.answer:
-- postgres
WITH with_gap AS (
    SELECT customer_id, id AS transaction_id, transaction_date,
    transaction_date - LAG(transaction_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS days_since_prev
    FROM transactions
    WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
),
with_session_flag AS (
    SELECT *,
    CASE
        WHEN days_since_prev IS NULL THEN 1  -- first tx = new session
        WHEN days_since_prev > 30 THEN 1     -- gap > 30 days = new session
        ELSE 0
    END AS new_session
    FROM with_gap
)
SELECT customer_id, transaction_id, transaction_date,
SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS session_number
FROM with_session_flag
ORDER BY customer_id, transaction_date;

cards.title: Exercise 1 — DAU + 3-Day Rolling Average (EXACT interview Q)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each day, show:
  - event_date
  - dau (daily active users = COUNT DISTINCT user_id)
  - rolling_3day_avg (average DAU over current + 2 previous days)

Expected output:
  2024-01-01 | 3 | 3.00     (only 1 day available)
  2024-01-02 | 3 | 3.00     (avg of 3, 3)
  2024-01-03 | 2 | 2.67     (avg of 3, 3, 2)
  2024-01-04 | 4 | 3.00     (avg of 3, 2, 4)
  2024-01-05 | 2 | 2.67     (avg of 2, 4, 2)
  2024-01-06 | 5 | 3.67     (avg of 4, 2, 5) -- corrected: u5 view still counts as active
  2024-01-07 | 1 | 2.67     (avg of 2, 5, 1)

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
with events as (
    select event_date
    , count(distinct user_id) as daily_active_users
    from daily_events
    group by event_date
)
select event_date, daily_active_users,
round(avg(daily_active_users) over(order by event_date rows between 2 preceding and current row)) as rolling_avg_daily_active_users
from events
order by event_date;

-- SOLUTION 1:
-- WITH daily_active AS (
--     SELECT
--         event_date,
--         COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau
--     FROM daily_events
--     GROUP BY event_date
-- )
-- SELECT
--     event_date,
--     dau,
--     ROUND(
--         AVG(dau) OVER (
--             ORDER BY event_date
--             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--         ), 2
--     ) AS rolling_3day_avg
-- FROM daily_active
-- ORDER BY event_date;
--
-- KEY: Step 1 = aggregate (CTE). Step 2 = window on aggregated result.
-- ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW = 3-day window.
-- At start, fewer than 3 days available — AVG handles automatically.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 2 — Running Total (Cumulative Sum)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each day, show cumulative total sales amount.
Only for product = 'Widget'.

Expected: running total grows each day.

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
select sale_date, amount,
sum(amount) over(order by sale_date
    rows between unbounded preceding and current row) as cumulative_total
from daily_sales
where product = 'Widget'
order by sale_date;

-- SOLUTION 2:
-- SELECT
--     sale_date,
--     amount,
--     SUM(amount) OVER (
--         ORDER BY sale_date
--         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--     ) AS cumulative_total
-- FROM daily_sales
-- WHERE product = 'Widget'
-- ORDER BY sale_date;
--
-- KEY: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING = from the very first row.
-- SUM() OVER(ORDER BY date) without ROWS clause = default is
-- RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (includes ties!).
-- ROWS is more predictable — always use ROWS explicitly.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 3 — Rolling Average PER GROUP (partitioned)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each product, compute 3-day rolling average of daily total sales.
Show: product, sale_date, daily_total, rolling_3day_avg

Hint: Need CTE to get daily total per product first,
      then window PARTITIONED BY product.

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
with product_daily as (
    select product, sale_date, sum(amount) as daily_total
    from daily_sales
    group by product, sale_date
)
select product, sale_date, daily_total,
round(avg(daily_total) over(partition by product order by sale_date rows between 2 preceding and current row), 2) as rolling_3day_avg
from product_daily
order by product, sale_date;

-- SOLUTION 3:
-- WITH product_daily AS (
--     SELECT
--         product,
--         sale_date,
--         SUM(amount) AS daily_total
--     FROM daily_sales
--     GROUP BY product, sale_date
-- )
-- SELECT
--     product,
--     sale_date,
--     daily_total,
--     ROUND(
--         AVG(daily_total) OVER (
--             PARTITION BY product
--             ORDER BY sale_date
--             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--         ), 2
--     ) AS rolling_3day_avg
-- FROM product_daily
-- ORDER BY product, sale_date;
--
-- KEY: PARTITION BY product = each product gets its own window.
-- Without PARTITION BY, window crosses all products (wrong!).
-- Same pattern as PySpark: Window.partitionBy("product").orderBy("date")

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 4 — Difference from Previous Day (LAG)
cards.prompt:
Task: For Widget in East region, show:
  - sale_date, amount, prev_day_amount, day_over_day_change

day_over_day_change = current amount - previous day amount
First row should show NULL for prev and change.

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
select sale_date, amount, 
lag(amount,1) over(order by sale_date) as prev_day_amount,
amount - lag(amount,1) over(order by sale_date) as day_over_day_change
from daily_sales
where product = 'Widget' and region = 'East'
order by sale_date;

-- SOLUTION 4:
-- SELECT
--     sale_date,
--     amount,
--     LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS prev_day_amount,
--     amount - LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS day_over_day_change
-- FROM daily_sales
-- WHERE product = 'Widget' AND region = 'East'
-- ORDER BY sale_date;
--
-- KEY: LAG(col, 1) = previous row's value.
-- LAG(col, 2) = 2 rows back.
-- LEAD(col, 1) = next row's value.
-- LAG returns NULL when no previous row exists.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 5 — Moving Min and Max (range detection)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each employee, show per day:
  - tasks_completed
  - min tasks in last 3 days
  - max tasks in last 3 days
  - "range" = max - min (volatility measure)

This is how you'd detect anomalies in pipeline metrics.

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
select employee_id, metric_date, tasks_completed,
min(tasks_completed) over(partition by employee_id order by metric_date rows between 2 preceding and current row) as min_3day,
max(tasks_completed) over(partition by employee_id order by metric_date rows between 2 preceding and current row) as max_3day,
max(tasks_completed) over(partition by employee_id order by metric_date rows between 2 preceding and current row) - min(tasks_completed) over(partition by employee_id order by metric_date rows between 2 preceding and current row) as range_3day
from employee_metrics
order by employee_id, metric_date;

select employee_id, metric_date, tasks_completed,
min(tasks_completed) over w as min_3day,
max(tasks_completed) over w as max_3day,
max(tasks_completed) over w - min(tasks_completed) over w as range_3day
from employee_metrics
window w as (partition by employee_id order by metric_date rows between 2 preceding and current row)
order by employee_id, metric_date;

-- SOLUTION 5:
-- SELECT
--     employee_id,
--     metric_date,
--     tasks_completed,
--     MIN(tasks_completed) OVER w AS min_3day,
--     MAX(tasks_completed) OVER w AS max_3day,
--     MAX(tasks_completed) OVER w - MIN(tasks_completed) OVER w AS range_3day
-- FROM employee_metrics
-- WINDOW w AS (
--     PARTITION BY employee_id
--     ORDER BY metric_date
--     ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
-- )
-- ORDER BY employee_id, metric_date;
--
-- KEY: Named window (WINDOW w AS ...) avoids repeating definition.
-- Works in PostgreSQL and Snowflake. Not all DBs support it.
-- Alternative: repeat the OVER clause for each function.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 6 — Rank + Running Count (combined)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each day, rank regions by total sales (highest = rank 1).
Also show running total per region across days.

Output columns: sale_date, region, daily_total, region_rank, running_total

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
select sale_date, region, daily_total,
rank() over(partition by sale_date order by daily_total desc) as region_rank,
sum(daily_total) over(partition by region order by sale_date rows between unbounded preceding and current row) as running_total
from (
    select sale_date, region, sum(amount) as daily_total
    from daily_sales
    group by sale_date, region
) as daily_region
order by sale_date, region_rank;

-- SOLUTION 6:
-- WITH daily_region AS (
--     SELECT
--         sale_date,
--         region,
--         SUM(amount) AS daily_total
--     FROM daily_sales
--     GROUP BY sale_date, region
-- )
-- SELECT
--     sale_date,
--     region,
--     daily_total,
--     RANK() OVER (
--         PARTITION BY sale_date
--         ORDER BY daily_total DESC
--     ) AS region_rank,
--     SUM(daily_total) OVER (
--         PARTITION BY region
--         ORDER BY sale_date
--         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--     ) AS running_total
-- FROM daily_region
-- ORDER BY sale_date, region_rank;
--
-- KEY: Two different windows in same query!
-- RANK: PARTITION BY sale_date (rank within each day)
-- Running total: PARTITION BY region (cumulate across days per region)
-- Different PARTITION BY = different grouping logic.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 7 — Percentage of Total (window vs subquery)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each sale, show:
  - amount
  - total for that product (across all dates/regions)
  - percentage of product total

Do it TWO ways:
  A) Using window function (SUM OVER)
  B) Using CTE + JOIN

YOUR QUERY HERE (Method A - Window):
cards.answer:
select sale_date, product, region, amount,
sum(amount) over(partition by product) as product_total,
round(amount * 100.0 / sum(amount) over(partition by product), 2) as pct_of_product
from daily_sales
order by product, sale_date;

-- YOUR QUERY HERE (Method B - CTE + JOIN):
with product_totals as (
    select product, sum(amount) as product_total
    from daily_sales
    group by product
)
select s.sale_date, s.product, s.region, s.amount,
t.product_total,
round(s.amount * 100.0 / t.product_total, 2) as pct_of_product
from daily_sales s
join product_totals t on s.product = t.product
order by s.product, s.sale_date;

-- SOLUTION 7A (Window):
-- SELECT
--     sale_date,
--     product,
--     region,
--     amount,
--     SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY product) AS product_total,
--     ROUND(
--         amount * 100.0 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY product), 2
--     ) AS pct_of_product
-- FROM daily_sales
-- ORDER BY product, sale_date;
--
-- SOLUTION 7B (CTE + JOIN):
-- WITH product_totals AS (
--     SELECT product, SUM(amount) AS product_total
--     FROM daily_sales
--     GROUP BY product
-- )
-- SELECT
--     s.sale_date,
--     s.product,
--     s.region,
--     s.amount,
--     t.product_total,
--     ROUND(s.amount * 100.0 / t.product_total, 2) AS pct_of_product
-- FROM daily_sales s
-- JOIN product_totals t ON s.product = t.product
-- ORDER BY s.product, s.sale_date;
--
-- KEY: Window without ORDER BY = entire partition (no frame).
-- SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY product) = total for that product.
-- Both methods produce same result. Window is more concise.
-- Interview: know both approaches.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 8 — Gap Detection (LEAD/LAG)
cards.prompt:
Task: Find days where a user was active, then INACTIVE
for 2+ days, then active again (gap detection).

For each user, show:
  - user_id
  - last_active_date (before gap)
  - next_active_date (after gap)
  - gap_days (difference)

Only show gaps >= 2 days.

YOUR QUERY HERE:
cards.answer:
select user_id, event_date as last_active_before_gap,
lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date) as next_active_date,
julianday(lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date)) - julianday(event_date) as gap_days
from (
    select distinct user_id, event_date
    from daily_events
) as user_dates
where (julianday(lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date)) - julianday(event_date)) >= 2
order by user_id, event_date;

with user_date as (
    select distinct user_id, event_date
    from daily_events
)
select user_id, event_date as last_active_before_gap,
lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date) as next_active_date,
julianday(lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date)) - julianday(event_date) as gap_days
from user_date
where (julianday(lead(event_date) over(partition by user_id order by event_date)) - julianday(event_date)) >= 2
order by user_id, event_date;

-- SOLUTION 8:
-- WITH user_dates AS (
--     SELECT DISTINCT user_id, event_date
--     FROM daily_events
-- ),
-- with_next AS (
--     SELECT
--         user_id,
--         event_date,
--         LEAD(event_date) OVER (
--             PARTITION BY user_id
--             ORDER BY event_date
--         ) AS next_active_date
--     FROM user_dates
-- )
-- SELECT
--     user_id,
--     event_date AS last_active_before_gap,
--     next_active_date,
--     (julianday(next_active_date) - julianday(event_date)) AS gap_days
--     -- PostgreSQL: next_active_date - event_date
--     -- Snowflake: DATEDIFF('day', event_date, next_active_date)
-- FROM with_next
-- WHERE (julianday(next_active_date) - julianday(event_date)) >= 2
-- ORDER BY user_id, event_date;
--
-- KEY: LEAD gives next row's value = next time user was active.
-- Difference = gap in days.
-- DISTINCT first to avoid same-day duplicates.
-- Real use case: detect churned users, SLA violations, pipeline gaps.

-- ============================================================
-- CHEAT SHEET: Window Frame Clauses
-- ============================================================
--
-- ROWS BETWEEN options:
--   UNBOUNDED PRECEDING  = from first row of partition
--   N PRECEDING          = N rows before current
--   CURRENT ROW          = current row
--   N FOLLOWING           = N rows after current
--   UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING  = to last row of partition
--
-- Common patterns:
--   Running total:     ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--   3-day rolling avg: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
--   Centered window:   ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
--   Entire partition:  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
--
-- ROWS vs RANGE:
--   ROWS  = physical rows (predictable, use this)
--   RANGE = logical value range (includes ties, can surprise you)
--
-- Functions that use frames: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT
-- Functions that DON'T use frames: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE
LAST_VALUE(salario) OVER (
    PARTITION BY departamento 
    ORDER BY data_contratacao
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING -- < Isso é o Frame!
)

cards.title: Exercise 1 — COPY INTO (Loading Data)
cards.prompt:
Task: Write COPY INTO statements for these scenarios.
You don't need to run these — just practice the syntax.

Scenario A: Load CSV from S3 into staging table
YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
create or replace stage my_s3_stage
    url = 's3://my-bucket/raw-data/'
    credentials = (aws_key_id='...' aws_secret_key='...')
    file_format = (type = 'csv' skip_header = 1 field_optionally_enclosed_by = '"');

copy into staging_events
from @my_s3_stage/events/2024/
pattern = '.*\.csv'
on_error = 'continue'        -- skip bad rows (log them)
force = false;               -- skip already-loaded files (idempotent!)

-- SOLUTION A:
-- -- First, create a stage pointing to S3
-- CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE my_s3_stage
--     URL = 's3://my-bucket/raw-data/'
--     CREDENTIALS = (AWS_KEY_ID='...' AWS_SECRET_KEY='...')
--     -- Better: use storage integration (no keys in SQL)
--     FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'CSV' SKIP_HEADER = 1 FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"');
--
-- -- Load data
-- COPY INTO staging_events
-- FROM @my_s3_stage/events/2024/
-- PATTERN = '.*\.csv'
-- ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'        -- skip bad rows (log them)
-- -- ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT' -- fail on first error (default)
-- FORCE = FALSE;               -- skip already-loaded files (idempotent!)
--
-- KEY:
-- FORCE = FALSE (default) = won't reload same file twice. IDEMPOTENT.
-- PATTERN = regex filter for files.
-- ON_ERROR controls behavior on bad rows.

-- Scenario B: Load Parquet from S3
-- YOUR QUERY:
copy into target_table
from @my_s3_stage/parquet-data/
file_format = (type = 'parquet')
match_by_column_name = case_insensitive
on_error = 'continue';  -- skip bad rows (log them)

-- SOLUTION B:
-- COPY INTO target_table
-- FROM @my_s3_stage/parquet-data/
-- FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET')
-- MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE
-- ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';
--
-- KEY: MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME maps Parquet columns to table columns by name.
-- No need to specify column order. Handles schema evolution gracefully.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 2 — MERGE (Upsert in Snowflake)
cards.prompt:
This is what they asked in the interview but in Snowflake!

Task: Write a MERGE that:
  - Updates existing records if incoming has newer updated_at
  - Inserts new records that don't exist
  - This is the Snowflake equivalent of Exercise 1 (Python upsert)

Setup (conceptual):
CREATE TABLE target_customers (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR,
    value DECIMAL(10,2),
    updated_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE staging_customers (LIKE target_customers);
-- Assume staging_customers has new data from COPY INTO

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
merge into target_customers t
using staging_customers s
on t.id = s.id
when matched and s.updated_at > t.updated_at then
    update set
        t.name = s.name,
        t.value = s.value,
        t.updated_at = s.updated_at
when not matched then
    insert (id, name, value, updated_at)
    values (s.id, s.name, s.value, s.updated_at);

-- SOLUTION 2:
-- MERGE INTO target_customers t
-- USING staging_customers s
-- ON t.id = s.id
-- WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN
--     UPDATE SET
--         t.name = s.name,
--         t.value = s.value,
--         t.updated_at = s.updated_at
-- WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
--     INSERT (id, name, value, updated_at)
--     VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.value, s.updated_at);
--
-- KEY:
-- MERGE = atomic upsert. No partial writes risk.
-- WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at = only update if newer.
-- This is how you avoid partial writes in Snowflake (interview Q3!).
-- After MERGE: TRUNCATE staging_customers (disposable).

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 3 — Time Travel & UNDROP
cards.prompt:
Snowflake keeps history for 0-90 days (Enterprise: 90, Standard: 1).
You can query data AS OF a previous point in time.

Task A: Someone accidentally deleted rows 30 minutes ago.
Write a query to see what the table looked like before deletion.
YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select * from target_customers
at (offset => -60*30);  -- 30 minutes ago in seconds
-- or
select * from target_customers
at (timestamp => '2024-01-15 10:00:00'::timestamp);

-- Task B: Someone dropped the entire table. Recover it.
-- YOUR QUERY:
insert into target_customers
select * from target_customers
at (offset => -60*30)  -- 30 minutes ago in seconds
where id not in (select id from target_customers);
-- or
undrop table target_customers;
-- SOLUTION 3A:
-- -- Query table as it was 30 minutes ago
-- SELECT * FROM target_customers
-- AT (OFFSET => -60*30);  -- 30 minutes ago in seconds
--
-- -- Or using timestamp:
-- SELECT * FROM target_customers
-- AT (TIMESTAMP => '2024-01-15 10:00:00'::TIMESTAMP);
--
-- -- Restore deleted rows:
-- INSERT INTO target_customers
-- SELECT * FROM target_customers
-- AT (OFFSET => -60*30)
-- WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM target_customers);

-- SOLUTION 3B:
-- UNDROP TABLE target_customers;
--
-- KEY:
-- Time Travel = query historical data without backups.
-- AT(OFFSET => -seconds) or AT(TIMESTAMP => 'time')
-- UNDROP = recover dropped tables, schemas, databases.
-- Retention period: DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS (default 1, up to 90).
--
-- INTERVIEW PHRASE:
-- "Snowflake Time Travel lets me recover from accidental deletes or
-- bad deployments without maintaining separate backups. I can query
-- the table as it was at any point in the retention window."

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 4 — Streams & Tasks (CDC in Snowflake)
cards.prompt:
Streams = track changes (inserts, updates, deletes) on a table.
Tasks = scheduled jobs (like Airflow tasks, but inside Snowflake).
Together = near-real-time CDC pipeline.

Task: Create a stream on source table, and a task that
processes changes every 5 minutes into a target table.
YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
create or replace stream events_stream
on table raw_events
show_initial_rows = false;   -- only new changes

create or replace task process_events
    warehouse = 'ETL_WH'
    schedule = '15 minute'
    when system$stream_has_data('events_stream')  -- only run if new data
as
    merge into processed_events t
    using events_stream s
    on t.event_id = s.event_id
    when matched and s.metadata$action = 'DELETE' and s.metadata$isupdate = false then
        delete
    when matched and s.metadata$action = 'UPDATE' then
        update set t.value = s.value, t.updated_at = current_timestamp()
    when not matched and s.metadata$action = 'INSERT' then
        insert (event_id, value, updated_at)
        values (s.event_id, s.value, current_timestamp());

alter task process_events resume;  -- tasks are created suspended by default
-- SOLUTION 4:
-- -- Step 1: Create stream (tracks changes)
-- CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM events_stream
-- ON TABLE raw_events
-- SHOW_INITIAL_ROWS = FALSE;   -- only new changes
--
-- -- Step 2: Create task (runs on schedule)
-- CREATE OR REPLACE TASK process_events
--     WAREHOUSE = 'ETL_WH'
--     SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
--     WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('events_stream')  -- only run if new data
-- AS
--     MERGE INTO processed_events t
--     USING events_stream s
--     ON t.event_id = s.event_id
--     WHEN MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
--         UPDATE SET t.value = s.value, t.updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
--     WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
--         INSERT (event_id, value, updated_at)
--         VALUES (s.event_id, s.value, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());
--
-- -- Step 3: Enable task (tasks are created suspended)
-- ALTER TASK process_events RESUME;
--
-- KEY:
-- Stream columns: METADATA$ACTION ('INSERT','DELETE'), METADATA$ISUPDATE
-- WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA = skip if no new changes (cost saving)
-- Tasks must be RESUMED to start running.
-- This replaces simple Airflow incremental loads — runs inside Snowflake.
--
-- INTERVIEW PHRASE:
-- "For near-real-time processing within Snowflake, I'd use Streams + Tasks.
-- Stream tracks CDC on the source, Task runs a MERGE every N minutes.
-- For more complex orchestration across systems, I'd still use Airflow."

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 5 — Warehouse Sizing & Cost Optimization
cards.prompt: No SQL here — conceptual questions they might ask.

cards.title: Q 1 — Your ETL runs daily at 6 AM and takes 2 hours on a Medium warehouse.
cards.prompt:
Boss asks to make it faster. What options do you have?

A1:
Option A: Scale UP — change to Large (2x compute, 2x cost, ~half time)
  ALTER WAREHOUSE etl_wh SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'LARGE';

Option B: Multi-cluster warehouse (auto-scale for concurrency)
  ALTER WAREHOUSE etl_wh SET MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3;
  (Better for concurrent queries, not single-query speed)

Option C: Optimize queries first (free!)
  - Check QUERY_HISTORY for slow queries
  - Add clustering keys on large filtered tables
  - Use RESULT_CACHE (automatic, queries < 24h repeated = free)
  - Avoid SELECT * — columnar storage benefits from column pruning

INTERVIEW PHRASE:
"Before scaling up the warehouse, I'd check QUERY_HISTORY to find
bottlenecks. Often it's a few slow queries that need clustering keys
or query rewrites. Scaling up is easy but doubles cost."

cards.title: Q 2 — Dashboards are slow during business hours but fast at night.
cards.prompt:
What's happening?

A2: Warehouse contention. Multiple dashboard queries compete for
    same warehouse resources.
Fix: Create separate warehouse for dashboards with auto-scaling.
  CREATE WAREHOUSE dashboard_wh
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL'
    AUTO_SUSPEND = 60          -- suspend after 1 min idle
    AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
    MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
    MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3;     -- auto-scale for concurrency

KEY: Separate warehouses for different workloads:
  - ETL_WH (Medium, scheduled, auto-suspend)
  - DASHBOARD_WH (Small, multi-cluster, always available)
  - ADHOC_WH (Small, auto-suspend aggressively)

cards.title: Exercise 6 — Snowflake-Specific SQL Features
cards.prompt:
6A: QUALIFY (filter window functions without CTE)
Task: Get latest record per user_id. One query, no CTE.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select * from events
qualify row_number() over (partition by user_id order by event_date desc) = 1;

-- SOLUTION 6A:
-- SELECT *
-- FROM events
-- QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_date DESC) = 1;
--
-- KEY: QUALIFY filters AFTER window function (like HAVING for GROUP BY).
-- Replaces CTE + WHERE rn = 1 pattern. Snowflake-specific (not in Postgres).
-- MUCH cleaner for dedup queries.

-- 6B: FLATTEN (explode nested JSON/arrays)
-- Task: You have a JSON column with nested array. Extract each element.

-- Setup:
-- CREATE TABLE api_responses (
--     id INT,
--     data VARIANT  -- Snowflake's JSON type
-- );
-- INSERT INTO api_responses SELECT 1, PARSE_JSON('{"tags": ["python", "sql", "spark"], "score": 95}');
-- INSERT INTO api_responses SELECT 2, PARSE_JSON('{"tags": ["java", "scala"], "score": 80}');

-- YOUR QUERY:
select
    r.id,
    r.data:score::INT AS score,
    f.value::STRING AS tag
from api_responses r,
    lateral flatten(input => r.data:tags) f;

-- SOLUTION 6B:
-- SELECT
--     r.id,
--     r.data:score::INT AS score,
--     f.value::STRING AS tag
-- FROM api_responses r,
--     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.data:tags) f;
--
-- Output:
-- 1 | 95 | python
-- 1 | 95 | sql
-- 1 | 95 | spark
-- 2 | 80 | java
-- 2 | 80 | scala
--
-- KEY:
-- VARIANT = semi-structured data type (JSON, Avro, XML, Parquet)
-- data:score = dot notation to access JSON fields
-- ::INT = cast to type
-- LATERAL FLATTEN = explode array (like PySpark explode())
-- This is how you handle nested API responses in Snowflake.

-- 6C: INSERT OVERWRITE (partition-level idempotency)
-- Task: Reload data for a specific date without duplicating.

-- YOUR QUERY:
insert overwrite into target_table
select * from staging_table
where event_date = '2024-01-15';

-- SOLUTION 6C:
-- INSERT OVERWRITE INTO target_table
-- SELECT * FROM staging_table
-- WHERE event_date = '2024-01-15';
--
-- KEY: INSERT OVERWRITE replaces matching partitions.
-- Idempotent: run twice = same result, no duplicates.
-- Alternative to DELETE + INSERT (atomic, no partial state).

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 7 — Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
cards.prompt:
Conceptual — common interview question.

Snowflake hierarchy:
  ACCOUNTADMIN → SECURITYADMIN → USERADMIN
               → SYSADMIN → custom roles → PUBLIC

Best practices:
  - Never use ACCOUNTADMIN for daily work
  - Create custom roles per team/function
  - Grant privileges to ROLES, not users
  - Users get roles, roles get privileges

Example:
CREATE ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE etl_wh TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE analytics TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA analytics.silver TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT ROLE data_engineer TO USER felipe;

INTERVIEW PHRASE:
"I follow least-privilege principle. Create specific roles per team,
grant only necessary privileges, never use ACCOUNTADMIN for ETL."

cards.title: Exercise 8 — Performance Debugging
cards.prompt:
Task: Query is slow. How do you debug in Snowflake?

Step 1: Check query profile
  SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY())
  WHERE QUERY_TEXT ILIKE '%my_table%'
  ORDER BY START_TIME DESC
  LIMIT 10;

Step 2: Look at Query Profile UI (Snowflake web)
  - Shows execution plan as graph
  - Identify: spilling to disk, exploding joins, full scans

Step 3: Check partition pruning
  SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('my_table', '(event_date)');
  -- Shows clustering depth and overlap

Common fixes:
| Problem                | Fix                                    |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Full table scan        | Add WHERE clause, clustering key       |
| Spilling to disk       | Scale up warehouse, reduce data volume |
| Exploding join         | Check join keys for duplicates         |
| Small files from stage | Use larger files (100-250MB)           |
| Network transfer       | Use same cloud region as data source   |

QUICK REFERENCE: Snowflake vs Other Systems

| Feature           | Snowflake           | Spark/EMR         | Postgres        |
|-------------------|---------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| Storage format    | Micro-partitions    | Parquet/Iceberg   | Heap/B-tree     |
| Compute scaling   | Warehouse resize    | Add nodes         | Vertical only   |
| Semi-structured   | VARIANT type        | StructType/JSON   | JSONB           |
| CDC               | Streams + Tasks     | Structured Stream | Triggers/WAL    |
| Time Travel       | Built-in (90 days)  | Iceberg snapshots | No (use backups)|
| Dedup syntax      | QUALIFY             | Window + filter   | CTE + WHERE     |
| Upsert            | MERGE INTO          | MERGE INTO        | ON CONFLICT     |
| Cost model        | Per-second compute  | Per-hour cluster  | Fixed server    |

INTERVIEW GOLD:
"Snowflake and Iceberg both offer time travel and schema evolution.
Key difference: Snowflake is fully managed — I don't manage storage
or compute infrastructure. With Iceberg on EMR, I have more control
but more operational overhead. I'd choose based on the team's needs."

cards.title: Section 1 — POSTGRESQL-SPECIFIC SYNTAX
cards.prompt: Things different from SQLite/Snowflake you already know

cards.title: Exercise 1 — DATE_TRUNC vs strftime
cards.prompt:
In SQLite you used strftime('%m', date). PostgreSQL uses DATE_TRUNC.

Task: Monthly transaction volume and total amount.
Show: month, tx_count, total_amount
Only completed transactions.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select date_trunc('month', requested_at) as month,
       count(*) as tx_count,
       round(sum(amount), 2) as total_amount
from transactions
where status = 'completed'
group by date_trunc('month', requested_at)
order by month;

-- SOLUTION 1:
-- SELECT
--     DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at) AS month,
--     COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
--     ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS total_amount
-- FROM transactions
-- WHERE status = 'completed'
-- GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at)
-- ORDER BY month;
--
-- KEY DIFFERENCES FROM SQLITE:
-- SQLite:    strftime('%Y-%m', date)           → returns STRING '2024-01'
-- Postgres:  DATE_TRUNC('month', timestamp)    → returns TIMESTAMP 2024-01-01 00:00:00
-- Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', date)         → same as Postgres
--
-- Also works: DATE_TRUNC('week', ...), DATE_TRUNC('quarter', ...)
-- EXTRACT(MONTH FROM requested_at) → returns integer 1-12

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 2 — INTERVAL arithmetic
cards.prompt:
Task: Find all transactions from last 30 days relative to
the most recent transaction in the table.
Show: tx_id, requested_at, amount, transfer_type

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select tx_id, requested_at, amount, transfer_type
from transactions
where requested_at >= (select max(requested_at) from transactions) - interval '30 days'
order by requested_at desc;

-- SOLUTION 2:
-- SELECT tx_id, requested_at, amount, transfer_type
-- FROM transactions
-- WHERE requested_at >= (SELECT MAX(requested_at) FROM transactions) - INTERVAL '30 days'
-- ORDER BY requested_at DESC;
--
-- KEY: PostgreSQL INTERVAL is powerful:
--   NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
--   NOW() - INTERVAL '2 hours 30 minutes'
--   date_column + INTERVAL '1 month'
--   AGE(timestamp1, timestamp2) → returns interval
--
-- SQLite: date('now', '-30 days')
-- Snowflake: DATEADD('day', -30, CURRENT_DATE())

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 3 — GENERATE_SERIES (no equivalent in SQLite!)
cards.prompt:
Task: Generate a calendar of all dates in 2024.
For each date, show transaction count (0 if no transactions).
Show: cal_date, is_weekend, tx_count

Hint: LEFT JOIN generate_series with transactions

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select d.cal_date,
       extract(dow from d.cal_date) in (0, 6) as is_weekend,
       count(t.tx_id) as tx_count
from generate_series(
         '2024-01-01'::date,
         '2024-12-31'::date,
         '1 day'::interval
        ) as d(cal_date)
left join transactions t
    on t.requested_at::date = d.cal_date
    and t.status = 'completed'
group by d.cal_date
order by d.cal_date;

-- SOLUTION 3:
-- SELECT
--     d.cal_date,
--     EXTRACT(DOW FROM d.cal_date) IN (0, 6) AS is_weekend,
--     COUNT(t.tx_id) AS tx_count
-- FROM generate_series(
--     '2024-01-01'::DATE,
--     '2024-12-31'::DATE,
--     '1 day'::INTERVAL
-- ) AS d(cal_date)
-- LEFT JOIN transactions t
--     ON t.requested_at::DATE = d.cal_date
--     AND t.status = 'completed'
-- GROUP BY d.cal_date
-- ORDER BY d.cal_date;
--
-- KEY: generate_series = inline table generator.
--   generate_series(1, 10)                → integers 1..10
--   generate_series(start_date, end_date, interval) → date sequence
-- EXTRACT(DOW FROM date): 0=Sunday, 6=Saturday
-- This replaces d_date dimension for ad-hoc analysis!

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 4 — FILTER clause (PostgreSQL exclusive!)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each account, in ONE query show:
  - total_tx
  - completed_count
  - failed_count
  - pix_amount (total amount of PIX only)
  - non_pix_amount (total amount of TED + DOC)

Use FILTER clause instead of CASE WHEN inside SUM.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select account_id, count(*) as total_tx,
       count(*) filter (where status = 'completed') as completed_count,
       count(*) filter (where status = 'failed') as failed_count,
       coalesce(sum(amount) filter (
        where transfer_type = 'pix' and status = 'completed'), 0)
         as pix_amount,
       coalesce(sum(amount) filter (
        where transfer_type in ('ted', 'doc') and status = 'completed'), 0)
         as non_pix_amount
from transactions
group by account_id
order by account_id;

-- SOLUTION 4:
-- SELECT
--     account_id,
--     COUNT(*) AS total_tx,
--     COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') AS completed_count,
--     COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failed_count,
--     COALESCE(SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE transfer_type = 'pix' AND status = 'completed'), 0) AS pix_amount,
--     COALESCE(SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE transfer_type IN ('ted', 'doc') AND status = 'completed'), 0) AS non_pix_amount
-- FROM transactions
-- GROUP BY account_id;
--
-- KEY: FILTER (WHERE condition) = cleaner than SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)
-- PostgreSQL-only! Not in Snowflake, not in SQLite.
-- Same result as: SUM(CASE WHEN status='completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
-- But much more readable, especially with multiple conditional aggregates.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 5 — JSONB queries (very Nubank!)
cards.prompt:
Task A: Find all transactions made via 'app' channel on 'ios' device.
Task B: Count transactions per channel.
Task C: Add a new key 'flagged' = true to metadata for failed transactions.

Remember: metadata column is JSONB

YOUR QUERY (A):
cards.answer:
select tx_id, amount, transfer_type, metadata
from transactions
where metadata->>'channel' = 'app'
  and metadata->>'device' = 'ios';

-- YOUR QUERY (B):
select
    metadata->>'channel' as channel,
    count(*) as tx_count,
    round(avg(amount), 2) as avg_amount
from transactions
group by metadata->>'channel';

-- YOUR QUERY (C - just write the UPDATE, don't run):
update transactions
set metadata = metadata || '{"flagged": true}'::jsonb
where status = 'failed';

-- Resumo prático:
-- -> = Navega no JSON e cospe JSON.
-- ->> = Navega no JSON e cospe Texto.
-- || entre Strings = Gruda textos.
-- || entre JSONBs = Faz o merge dos objetos (adiciona ou atualiza chaves).

-- SOLUTION 5A:
-- SELECT tx_id, amount, transfer_type, metadata
-- FROM transactions
-- WHERE metadata->>'channel' = 'app'
--   AND metadata->>'device' = 'ios';
--
-- SOLUTION 5B:
-- SELECT
--     metadata->>'channel' AS channel,
--     COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
--     ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount
-- FROM transactions
-- GROUP BY metadata->>'channel';
--
-- SOLUTION 5C:
-- UPDATE transactions
-- SET metadata = metadata || '{"flagged": true}'::JSONB
-- WHERE status = 'failed';
--
-- KEY JSONB OPERATORS:
--   ->   access key, returns JSONB:    metadata->'channel'
--   ->>  access key, returns TEXT:     metadata->>'channel'
--   @>   contains:                     metadata @> '{"channel": "app"}'
--   ||   merge/concatenate:            metadata || '{"new_key": "val"}'
--   -    remove key:                   metadata - 'old_key'
--   #>   path access:                  metadata#>'{nested,key}'
--
-- GIN INDEX for fast JSONB queries:
--   CREATE INDEX idx_tx_metadata ON transactions USING GIN (metadata);

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Section 2 — COMMON INTERVIEW PATTERNS (PostgreSQL syntax)
cards.prompt: COMMON INTERVIEW PATTERNS (PostgreSQL syntax)

cards.title: Exercise 6 — Running Balance (account statement)
cards.prompt:
Task: For a given account, calculate running balance.
Money IN = positive, money OUT = negative.
Show: requested_at, transfer_type, direction, amount, signed_amount, running_balance
Only completed transactions. Order by time.

Pick any account_id from: SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1;

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
with signed_tx as (
    select requested_at, transfer_type, direction, amount,
           case when direction = 'in' 
           then amount else -amount end as signed_amount
    from transactions
    where account_id = (select account_id from accounts limit 1)
      and status = 'completed'
)
select requested_at, transfer_type, direction, amount, signed_amount,
       sum(signed_amount) over (order by requested_at) as running_balance
from signed_tx
order by requested_at;

-- SOLUTION 6:
-- WITH signed_tx AS (
--     SELECT
--         requested_at,
--         transfer_type,
--         direction,
--         amount,
--         CASE WHEN direction = 'in' THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS signed_amount
--     FROM transactions
--     WHERE account_id = (SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1)
--       AND status = 'completed'
-- )
-- SELECT
--     requested_at,
--     transfer_type,
--     direction,
--     amount,
--     signed_amount,
--     SUM(signed_amount) OVER (ORDER BY requested_at) AS running_balance
-- FROM signed_tx
-- ORDER BY requested_at;
--
-- KEY: Classic fintech pattern. Every bank interview asks this.
-- SUM() OVER (ORDER BY time) = running total = running balance.
-- CASE direction to make amounts signed (+in / -out).

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 7 — Cohort Analysis (retention)
cards.prompt:
Task: Monthly retention cohort.
For each customer's signup month (cohort), count how many
were still transacting in each subsequent month.

Show: cohort_month, months_since_signup, active_customers

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
with cohorts as (
    select customer_id,
           date_trunc('month', created_at)::date as cohort_month
    from customers
),
activity as (
    select distinct a.customer_id,
           date_trunc('month', t.requested_at)::date as active_month
    from transactions t
    join accounts a using (account_id)
    where t.status = 'completed'
)
select c.cohort_month,
       extract(year from age(act.active_month, c.cohort_month)) * 12 +
       extract(month from age(act.active_month, c.cohort_month)) as months_since_signup,
       count(distinct c.customer_id) as active_customers
from cohorts c
join activity act using (customer_id)
where act.active_month >= c.cohort_month
group by c.cohort_month, months_since_signup
order by c.cohort_month, months_since_signup;

-- SOLUTION 7:
-- WITH cohorts AS (
--     SELECT
--         customer_id,
--         DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)::DATE AS cohort_month
--     FROM customers
-- ),
-- activity AS (
--     SELECT DISTINCT
--         a.customer_id,
--         DATE_TRUNC('month', t.requested_at)::DATE AS active_month
--     FROM transactions t
--     JOIN accounts a USING (account_id)
--     WHERE t.status = 'completed'
-- )
-- SELECT
--     c.cohort_month,
--     EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(act.active_month, c.cohort_month)) * 12 +
--     EXTRACT(MONTH FROM AGE(act.active_month, c.cohort_month)) AS months_since_signup,
--     COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS active_customers
-- FROM cohorts c
-- JOIN activity act USING (customer_id)
-- WHERE act.active_month >= c.cohort_month
-- GROUP BY c.cohort_month, months_since_signup
-- ORDER BY c.cohort_month, months_since_signup;
--
-- KEY: AGE(date1, date2) returns INTERVAL. Extract months from it.
-- DISTINCT on customer+month avoids double counting.
-- This is THE classic analytics engineer interview question.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 8 — LATERAL JOIN (PostgreSQL power feature)
cards.prompt:
Task: For each customer, get their 3 most recent transactions.
Show: customer name, tx amount, transfer_type, requested_at

Use LATERAL JOIN (more efficient than window + filter for top-N per group)

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select c.full_name, lat.amount, lat.transfer_type, lat.requested_at
from customers c
join accounts a on a.customer_id = c.customer_id
cross join lateral (
    select t.amount, t.transfer_type, t.requested_at
    from transactions t
    where t.account_id = a.account_id
      and t.status = 'completed'
    order by t.requested_at desc
    limit 3 
) lat
order by c.full_name, lat.requested_at desc;

-- SOLUTION 8:
-- SELECT
--     c.full_name,
--     lat.amount,
--     lat.transfer_type,
--     lat.requested_at
-- FROM customers c
-- JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
-- CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
--     SELECT t.amount, t.transfer_type, t.requested_at
--     FROM transactions t
--     WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
--       AND t.status = 'completed'
--     ORDER BY t.requested_at DESC
--     LIMIT 3
-- ) lat;
--
-- KEY: LATERAL = subquery can reference outer query columns.
-- Like a correlated subquery but returns multiple rows.
-- More efficient than ROW_NUMBER() OVER(...) for top-N per group
-- because it can use indexes and stop early (LIMIT).
--
-- Snowflake equivalent: LATERAL FLATTEN (different use case)
-- SQLite: no LATERAL support

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 9 — CTE + RECURSIVE (hierarchical data)
cards.prompt:
Task: Given a referral chain (customer A referred B, B referred C),
find all customers downstream of a given referrer.
This tests recursive CTE which is common in PostgreSQL interviews.
cards.answer:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS referrals;
CREATE TABLE referrals (
    customer_id UUID REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    referred_by UUID REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);

-- Build a referral chain: Ana → Bruno → Carlos → Diana
INSERT INTO referrals
SELECT c2.customer_id, c1.customer_id
FROM customers c1, customers c2
WHERE c1.full_name = 'Ana Silva' AND c2.full_name = 'Bruno Costa';

INSERT INTO referrals
SELECT c2.customer_id, c1.customer_id
FROM customers c1, customers c2
WHERE c1.full_name = 'Bruno Costa' AND c2.full_name = 'Carlos Mendes';

INSERT INTO referrals
SELECT c2.customer_id, c1.customer_id
FROM customers c1, customers c2
WHERE c1.full_name = 'Carlos Mendes' AND c2.full_name = 'Diana Rocha';

INSERT INTO referrals
SELECT c2.customer_id, c1.customer_id
FROM customers c1, customers c2
WHERE c1.full_name = 'Ana Silva' AND c2.full_name = 'Eduardo Lima';

-- Task: Find ALL customers referred directly or indirectly by Ana Silva.
-- Show: level (depth), customer name, referred by name

-- YOUR QUERY:
with recursive referral_chain as (
    -- Base case: direct referrals of Ana
    select r.customer_id, r.referred_by, 1 as level
    from referrals r
    join customers c on c.customer_id = r.referred_by
    where c.full_name = 'Ana Silva'
    
    union all
    
    -- Recursive case: referrals of referrals
    select r.customer_id, r.referred_by, rc.level + 1
    from referrals r
    join referral_chain rc on r.referred_by = rc.customer_id
    where rc.level < 10 -- safety check to prevent infinite recursion
)
select rc.level, c.full_name as customer_name, 
ref.full_name as referred_by_name
from referral_chain rc
join customers c on c.customer_id = rc.customer_id
join customers ref on ref.customer_id = rc.referred_by
order by rc.level, c.full_name;

-- SOLUTION 9:
-- WITH RECURSIVE referral_chain AS (
--     -- Base: Ana's direct referrals
--     SELECT
--         r.customer_id,
--         r.referred_by,
--         1 AS level
--     FROM referrals r
--     JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = r.referred_by
--     WHERE c.full_name = 'Ana Silva'
--
--     UNION ALL
--
--     -- Recursive: referrals of referrals
--     SELECT
--         r.customer_id,
--         r.referred_by,
--         rc.level + 1
--     FROM referrals r
--     JOIN referral_chain rc ON r.referred_by = rc.customer_id
-- )
-- SELECT
--     rc.level,
--     c.full_name AS customer_name,
--     ref.full_name AS referred_by_name
-- FROM referral_chain rc
-- JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = rc.customer_id
-- JOIN customers ref ON ref.customer_id = rc.referred_by
-- ORDER BY rc.level, c.full_name;
--
-- Expected:

cards.title: Level 1 — Bruno Costa (by Ana), Eduardo Lima (by Ana)
cards.prompt: Bruno Costa (by Ana), Eduardo Lima (by Ana)

cards.title: Level 2 — Carlos Mendes (by Bruno)
cards.prompt: Carlos Mendes (by Bruno)

cards.title: Level 3 — Diana Rocha (by Carlos)
cards.prompt:
KEY: WITH RECURSIVE = iterative until no more rows.
Base case UNION ALL recursive case.
Add LIMIT or max depth check to prevent infinite loops.
Snowflake: also supports RECURSIVE CTE.
SQLite: supports it too, but rarely tested in interviews.

cards.title: Exercise 10 — DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL exclusive!)
cards.prompt:
Task: Get most recent transaction per account. ONE line, no CTE.

DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL-only and replaces ROW_NUMBER() pattern.
Snowflake uses QUALIFY, Postgres uses DISTINCT ON.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select distinct on (account_id) account_id, 
tx_id, amount, transfer_type, status, requested_at
from transactions
order by account_id, requested_at desc;

-- SOLUTION 10:
-- SELECT DISTINCT ON (account_id)
--     account_id,
--     tx_id,
--     amount,
--     transfer_type,
--     status,
--     requested_at
-- FROM transactions
-- ORDER BY account_id, requested_at DESC;
--
-- KEY: DISTINCT ON (cols) keeps FIRST row per group based on ORDER BY.
-- ORDER BY must start with same columns as DISTINCT ON.
-- Much simpler than: ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY requested_at DESC) = 1
--
-- Snowflake: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER(...) = 1
-- PostgreSQL: DISTINCT ON (...)
-- Both = get first row per group. Know both syntaxes!

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 11 — Transaction validation with business rules
cards.prompt:
Task: Find invalid transactions based on transfer_limits rules:
  1. DOC with amount > 4999.99
  2. TED/DOC sent on weekend
  3. TED sent after 17:00
  4. DOC sent after 22:00

Show: tx_id, transfer_type, amount, requested_at, violation_reason

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select tx_id, transfer_type, amount, requested_at,
       case
           when transfer_type = 'doc' and amount > 4999.99
               then 'DOC exceeds R$4,999.99 limit'
           when transfer_type in ('ted', 'doc') and extract(dow from requested_at) in (0, 6)
               then 'Non-PIX transfer on weekend'
           when transfer_type = 'ted' and requested_at::time > '17:00'::time
               then 'TED after 17:00 cutoff'
           when transfer_type = 'doc' and requested_at::time > '22:00'::time
               then 'DOC after 22:00 cutoff'
       end as violation_reason
from transactions
where (transfer_type = 'doc' and amount > 4999.99)
   or (transfer_type in ('ted', 'doc') and extract(dow from requested_at) in (0, 6))
   or (transfer_type = 'ted' and requested_at::time > '17:00'::time)
   or (transfer_type = 'doc' and requested_at::time > '22:00'::time)
order by requested_at;

-- SOLUTION 11:
-- SELECT
--     t.tx_id,
--     t.transfer_type,
--     t.amount,
--     t.requested_at,
--     CASE
--         WHEN t.transfer_type = 'doc' AND t.amount > 4999.99
--             THEN 'DOC exceeds R$4,999.99 limit'
--         WHEN t.transfer_type IN ('ted', 'doc')
--              AND EXTRACT(DOW FROM t.requested_at) IN (0, 6)
--             THEN 'Non-PIX transfer on weekend'
--         WHEN t.transfer_type = 'ted'
--              AND t.requested_at::TIME > '17:00'::TIME
--             THEN 'TED after 17:00 cutoff'
--         WHEN t.transfer_type = 'doc'
--              AND t.requested_at::TIME > '22:00'::TIME
--             THEN 'DOC after 22:00 cutoff'
--     END AS violation_reason
-- FROM transactions t
-- WHERE (t.transfer_type = 'doc' AND t.amount > 4999.99)
--    OR (t.transfer_type IN ('ted', 'doc') 
--      AND EXTRACT(DOW FROM t.requested_at) IN (0, 6)
--    )
--    OR (t.transfer_type = 'ted' AND t.requested_at::TIME > '17:00'::TIME)
--    OR (t.transfer_type = 'doc' AND t.requested_at::TIME > '22:00'::TIME)
-- ORDER BY t.requested_at;
--
-- KEY: This connects your Nubank case knowledge!
-- ::TIME cast extracts time portion.
-- EXTRACT(DOW FROM ...) for day of week.
-- Real scenario: data quality check on transaction pipeline.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 12 — EXPLAIN ANALYZE (performance)
cards.prompt:
Task: Know how to read a query plan. They may ask you to optimize.

Run this and interpret the output:
cards.answer:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = (SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1)
   AND requested_at >= '2024-01-01'
   AND status = 'completed';
--
-- Then create appropriate indexes:

-- YOUR QUERY (create indexes):
create index idx_tx_account_date on transactions (account_id, requested_at desc);
-- partial (completed)
create index idx_tx_completed on transactions (account_id, requested_at desc)
where status = 'completed';

-- SOLUTION 12:
-- -- Composite index for common query pattern
-- CREATE INDEX idx_tx_account_date ON transactions (account_id, requested_at DESC);
--
-- -- Partial index for completed transactions only (smaller, faster)
-- CREATE INDEX idx_tx_completed ON transactions (account_id, requested_at DESC)
-- WHERE status = 'completed';
--
-- -- GIN index for JSONB queries
-- CREATE INDEX idx_tx_metadata ON transactions USING GIN (metadata);
--
-- KEY EXPLAIN ANALYZE terms:
--   Seq Scan    = full table scan (bad for big tables)
--   Index Scan  = using index (good)
--   Bitmap Scan = index → bitmap → heap (good for many rows)
--   Hash Join   = building hash table for join
--   Nested Loop = for each row in A, scan B (OK if B is small)
--   Sort        = explicit sort (check if index can avoid)
--   actual time = real execution time (ms)
--   rows        = actual rows processed
--
-- PARTIAL INDEX = index with WHERE clause. Smaller + faster.
-- Very PostgreSQL. Snowflake doesn't have user-managed indexes.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Section 3 — QUICK FIRE — Things They Might Ask
cards.prompt: QUICK FIRE — Things They Might Ask

cards.title: Q 1 — What's the difference between NUMERIC and FLOAT in PostgreSQL?
cards.prompt:
NUMERIC(15,2) = exact decimal (use for money!)
FLOAT/DOUBLE = approximate (binary floating point)
NEVER use FLOAT for financial data: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in FLOAT
Nubank cares about this — they handle money.

cards.title: Q 2 — DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
cards.prompt:
DELETE FROM t WHERE ...  → logged, can rollback, slow for full table
TRUNCATE TABLE t         → not logged per row, instant, resets sequences
DROP TABLE t             → removes table entirely

TRUNCATE is transactional in PostgreSQL (can rollback!)
This is different from MySQL where TRUNCATE is auto-commit.

cards.title: Q 3 — What is MVCC?
cards.prompt:
Multi-Version Concurrency Control.
Readers don't block writers. Writers don't block readers.
Each transaction sees a snapshot of data.
PostgreSQL keeps old row versions until VACUUM cleans them.

INTERVIEW PHRASE:
"PostgreSQL uses MVCC so reads never block writes. Each transaction
sees a consistent snapshot. Dead tuples are cleaned by autovacuum."

cards.title: Q 4 — ON CONFLICT (PostgreSQL upsert)
cards.prompt:
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, full_name, tax_id)
VALUES ('...', 'New Name', '12345678901')
ON CONFLICT (tax_id)
DO UPDATE SET full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name;

ON CONFLICT = PostgreSQL's MERGE equivalent.
EXCLUDED = the row that was rejected.
Snowflake: MERGE INTO ... WHEN MATCHED ... WHEN NOT MATCHED
PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE/NOTHING

cards.title: Q 5 — Common Table Expressions (CTE) - materialized vs not
cards.prompt:
PostgreSQL 12+: CTEs are NOT materialized by default (inlined).
Before PG 12: CTEs were always materialized (optimization fence).

Force materialization:
WITH my_cte AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...)

Force inlining:
WITH my_cte AS NOT MATERIALIZED (SELECT ...)

When to materialize: CTE used multiple times, expensive subquery.
When to inline: CTE used once, let planner optimize.

cards.title: Q 6 — STRING_AGG (PostgreSQL's GROUP_CONCAT)
cards.prompt:
SELECT
    account_id,
    STRING_AGG(transfer_type, ', ' ORDER BY requested_at) AS tx_types
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY account_id;

STRING_AGG supports ORDER BY inside! MySQL GROUP_CONCAT does too,
but this syntax is standard SQL.

cards.title: Q 7 — COALESCE vs NULLIF vs GREATEST vs LEAST
cards.prompt:
COALESCE(a, b, c)     → first non-null value
NULLIF(a, b)          → NULL if a=b, else a
GREATEST(a, b, c)     → max value (NULL-safe in PG)
LEAST(a, b, c)        → min value (NULL-safe in PG)

Common pattern: avoid division by zero
SELECT amount / NULLIF(count, 0) AS avg_per_count;

CHEAT SHEET: PostgreSQL vs SQLite vs Snowflake

| Feature            | PostgreSQL           | SQLite              | Snowflake           |
|--------------------|----------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Date truncate      | DATE_TRUNC('m', d)   | strftime('%Y-%m',d) | DATE_TRUNC('m', d)  |
| Date arithmetic    | d + INTERVAL '1 day' | date(d, '+1 day')   | DATEADD('day',1,d)  |
| Date diff          | d1 - d2 (integer)    | julianday(d1)-jd(d2)| DATEDIFF('d',d1,d2) |
| Day of week        | EXTRACT(DOW FROM d)  | strftime('%w', d)   | DAYOFWEEK(d)        |
| Upsert             | ON CONFLICT          | ON CONFLICT         | MERGE INTO          |
| Top-N per group    | DISTINCT ON          | ROW_NUMBER()        | QUALIFY             |
| Type cast          | value::TYPE          | CAST(v AS TYPE)     | value::TYPE         |
| JSON access        | col->>'key'          | json_extract(c,'$') | col:key             |
| Generate sequence  | generate_series()    | (recursive CTE)     | GENERATOR()         |
| Conditional agg    | FILTER (WHERE ...)   | CASE WHEN           | CASE WHEN           |
| String concat agg  | STRING_AGG()         | GROUP_CONCAT()      | LISTAGG()           |
| Regex match        | col ~ 'pattern'      | (not built-in)      | REGEXP_LIKE()       |
| Boolean type       | TRUE/FALSE           | 1/0                 | TRUE/FALSE          |
| UUID generation     | gen_random_uuid()    | (extension needed)  | UUID_STRING()       |
| Partial index      | CREATE INDEX ... WHERE| Not supported      | Not supported       |
| EXPLAIN            | EXPLAIN ANALYZE      | EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN  | (Query Profile UI)  |

cards.title: Exercise 1 — Funnel Analysis (Conversion Rates)
cards.prompt:
Task: Calculate PIX funnel: initiated -> completed -> reversed
For each month, show:
  - total_initiated (all statuses)
  - total_completed
  - total_failed
  - completion_rate (completed / initiated)
  - failure_rate (failed / initiated)

Format rates as percentage with 1 decimal.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select date_trunc('month', requested_at) as month,
    count(*) as total_initiated,
    count(*) filter (where status = 'completed') as total_completed,
    count(*) filter (where status = 'failed') as total_failed,
    round(100.0 * count(*) filter (where status = 'completed') / count(*), 1) as completion_rate,
    round(100.0 * count(*) filter (where status = 'failed') / count(*), 1) as failure_rate
from transactions
where transfer_type = 'pix'
group by date_trunc('month', requested_at)
order by month;

-- SOLUTION 1:
-- SELECT
--     DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at) AS month,
--     COUNT(*) AS total_initiated,
--     COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') AS total_completed,
--     COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS total_failed,
--     ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') / COUNT(*), 1) AS completion_rate,
--     ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') / COUNT(*), 1) AS failure_rate
-- FROM transactions
-- WHERE transfer_type = 'pix'
-- GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at)
-- ORDER BY month;
--
-- KEY: FILTER clause makes conditional aggregation readable.
-- 100.0 * forces float division (avoid integer division truncation).
-- This is a standard product analytics query.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 2 — Gap Detection (Missing Dates)
cards.prompt:
Task: Find dates where a specific account had NO transactions
but had transactions on both the day before AND the day after.
These are "suspicious gaps" worth investigating.

Steps:
  1. Get distinct transaction dates per account
  2. Use LAG/LEAD to find consecutive dates
  3. Where gap > 1 day, generate the missing dates

Pick account: SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1;

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
with account_date as (
    select distinct requested_at::date as tx_date
    from transactions
    where account_id = (select account_id from accounts limit 1)
    and status = 'completed'
    order by tx_date
), gaps as (
    select tx_date,
    lead(tx_date) over (order by tx_date) as next_date,
    lead(tx_date) over (order by tx_date) - tx_date as gap_days
    from account_date
)
select tx_date as gap_after,
next_date as gap_before,
gap_days - 1 as missing_days
from gaps
where gap_days > 1
order by tx_date;

-- Filter out weekends from missing dates
WITH account_date AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT requested_at::DATE AS tx_date
    FROM transactions
    WHERE account_id = (SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1)
      AND status = 'completed'
), gaps AS (
    SELECT tx_date,
           LEAD(tx_date) OVER (ORDER BY tx_date) AS next_date,
           LEAD(tx_date) OVER (ORDER BY tx_date) - tx_date AS gap_days
    FROM account_date
)
SELECT 
    g.tx_date AS gap_after,
    d.missing_date,
    TO_CHAR(d.missing_date, 'Day') AS day_name
FROM gaps g
-- Real banks have a holiday calendar table
AND d.missing_date NOT IN (
    SELECT holiday_date FROM bank_holidays
    WHERE country = 'BR'
)
AND EXTRACT(DOW FROM d.missing_date) NOT IN (0, 6)
/*
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(
    g.tx_date + 1,
    g.next_date - 1,
    '1 day'::INTERVAL
) AS d(missing_date)
WHERE g.gap_days > 1
  AND EXTRACT(DOW FROM d.missing_date) NOT IN (0, 6)  -- exclude Sun(0), Sat(6)
ORDER BY d.missing_date;
*/

-- SOLUTION 2:
-- WITH account_dates AS (
--     SELECT DISTINCT requested_at::DATE AS tx_date
--     FROM transactions
--     WHERE account_id = (SELECT account_id FROM accounts LIMIT 1)
--       AND status = 'completed'
--     ORDER BY tx_date
-- ),
-- gaps AS (
--     SELECT
--         tx_date,
--         LEAD(tx_date) OVER (ORDER BY tx_date) AS next_date,
--         LEAD(tx_date) OVER (ORDER BY tx_date) - tx_date AS gap_days
--     FROM account_dates
-- )
-- SELECT
--     tx_date AS gap_after,
--     next_date AS gap_before,
--     gap_days - 1 AS missing_days
-- FROM gaps
-- WHERE gap_days > 1
-- ORDER BY tx_date;
--
-- BONUS: Generate the actual missing dates:
-- SELECT
--     g.tx_date AS gap_after,
--     d.missing_date
-- FROM gaps g
-- CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(
--     g.tx_date + 1,
--     g.next_date - 1,
--     '1 day'::INTERVAL
-- ) AS d(missing_date)
-- WHERE g.gap_days > 1;
--
-- KEY: LEAD() looks ahead. gap = next_date - current_date.
-- generate_series fills in the actual missing dates.
-- Real use: data quality monitoring, SLA breach detection.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 3 — Sessionization (Activity Windows)
cards.prompt:
Task: Group transactions into "sessions" per account.
A session ends when there's a gap of > 30 minutes between
consecutive transactions.

Show: account_id, session_id, session_start, session_end,
      tx_count, total_amount

This is the EXACT same logic as Google Analytics sessions.

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
with ordered_tx as (
    select
        account_id,
        tx_id,
        amount,
        requested_at,
        lag(requested_at) over (partition by account_id order by requested_at) as prev_at
    from transactions
    where status = 'completed'
), session_starts as (
    select
        *,
        case
            when prev_at is null
              or requested_at - prev_at > interval '30 minutes'
            then 1
            else 0
        end as is_new_session
    from ordered_tx
), sessions as (
    select
        *,
        sum(is_new_session) over (
            partition by account_id order by requested_at
        ) as session_id
    from session_starts
)
select
    account_id,
    session_id,
    min(requested_at) as session_start,
    max(requested_at) as session_end,
    count(*) as tx_count,
    sum(amount) as total_amount
from sessions
group by account_id, session_id
order by account_id, session_start;

-- SOLUTION 3:
-- WITH ordered_tx AS (
--     SELECT
--         account_id,
--         tx_id,
--         amount,
--         requested_at,
--         LAG(requested_at) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY requested_at) AS prev_at
--     FROM transactions
--     WHERE status = 'completed'
-- ),
-- session_starts AS (
--     SELECT
--         *,
--         CASE
--             WHEN prev_at IS NULL
--               OR requested_at - prev_at > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
--             THEN 1
--             ELSE 0
--         END AS is_new_session
--     FROM ordered_tx
-- ),
-- sessions AS (
--     SELECT
--         *,
--         SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
--             PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY requested_at
--         ) AS session_id
--     FROM session_starts
-- )
-- SELECT
--     account_id,
--     session_id,
--     MIN(requested_at) AS session_start,
--     MAX(requested_at) AS session_end,
--     COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
--     SUM(amount) AS total_amount
-- FROM sessions
-- GROUP BY account_id, session_id
-- ORDER BY account_id, session_start;
--
-- KEY: Three-step pattern:
--   1. LAG to get previous timestamp
--   2. Flag new sessions (gap > threshold)
--   3. Running SUM of flags = session ID
-- This is sessionization — used in clickstream, fraud detection, UX analysis.
-- SUM(flag) OVER (ORDER BY time) = cumulative session counter.

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 4 — Percentile & Distribution Analysis
cards.prompt:
Task: For each transfer_type, calculate:
  - p50 (median), p75, p90, p99 of transaction amount
  - average amount
  - count

Use PERCENTILE_CONT (ordered-set aggregate).

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
select transfer_type, count(*) as tx_count,
    round(avg(amount), 2) as avg_amount,
    percentile_cont(0.50) within group (order by amount) as p50,
    percentile_cont(0.75) within group (order by amount) as p75,
    percentile_cont(0.90) within group (order by amount) as p90,
    percentile_cont(0.99) within group (order by amount) as p99
from transactions
where status = 'completed'
group by transfer_type
order by transfer_type;

-- SOLUTION 4:
-- SELECT
--     transfer_type,
--     COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
--     ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount,
--     PERCENTILE_CONT(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS p50,
--     PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS p75,
--     PERCENTILE_CONT(0.90) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS p90,
--     PERCENTILE_CONT(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS p99
-- FROM transactions
-- WHERE status = 'completed'
-- GROUP BY transfer_type
-- ORDER BY transfer_type;
--
-- KEY: PERCENTILE_CONT = continuous percentile (interpolates).
-- PERCENTILE_DISC = discrete (picks actual value from data).
-- WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) = ordered-set aggregate syntax.
-- Use case: SLA monitoring (p99 latency), amount thresholds for fraud.
-- Snowflake: APPROX_PERCENTILE (faster but approximate).

-- ============================================================

cards.title: Exercise 5 — Cumulative Distinct Count
cards.prompt:
Task: For each day, show the CUMULATIVE number of unique
customers who have ever transacted (running distinct count).

This is NOT a simple running count — a customer who transacts
on day 1 and day 5 should only be counted ONCE.

Show: date, new_customers_today, cumulative_unique_customers

YOUR QUERY:
cards.answer:
with first_tx as (
    select
        a.customer_id,
        min(t.requested_at::date) as first_tx_date
    from transactions t
    join accounts a using (account_id)
    where t.status = 'completed'
    group by a.customer_id
), daily_new as (
    select
        first_tx_date as tx_date,
        count(*) as new_customers
    from first_tx
    group by first_tx_date
)
select
    tx_date,
    new_customers as new_customers_today,
    sum(new_customers) over (order by tx_date) as cumulative_unique_customers
from daily_new
order by tx_date;

-- SOLUTION 5:
-- WITH first_tx AS (
--     SELECT
--         a.customer_id,
--         MIN(t.requested_at::DATE) AS first_tx_date
--     FROM transactions t
--     JOIN accounts a USING (account_id)
--     WHERE t.status = 'completed'
--     GROUP BY a.customer_id
-- ),
-- daily_new AS (
--     SELECT
--         first_tx_date AS tx_date,
--         COUNT(*) AS new_customers
--     FROM first_tx
--     GROUP BY first_tx_date
-- )
-- SELECT
--     tx_date,
