cards.prompt: Reference — Airflow — All Arguments Reference
cards.answer:
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  AIRFLOW ARGUMENTS — COMPLETE REFERENCE                                     ║
║  Every parameter you need to know, explained for interview depth.           ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. DEFAULT_ARGS — applied to every task in the DAG
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

DEFAULT_ARGS = {
    "owner": "data-engineering",
    "depends_on_past": False,
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),
    "retry_exponential_backoff": True,
    "max_retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=30),
    "email_on_failure": True,
    "email_on_retry": False,
    "email": ["team@company.com"],
    "execution_timeout": timedelta(hours=2),
    "sla": timedelta(hours=4),
}

PARAMETER                     DEFAULT        EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

owner                         "airflow"      Who owns this DAG. Shows in UI.
                                             Used for filtering and access control.
                                             Set to your team name.

depends_on_past               False          If True: task only runs if the SAME
                                             task in the PREVIOUS dag run succeeded.
                                             ⚠️ DANGER: one failure blocks ALL future
                                             runs until manually cleared.
                                             Almost always set to False.
                                             → "I keep runs independent. One bad Monday
                                               doesn't block Tuesday."

retries                       0              How many times to retry a failed task.
                                             0 = no retry, fail immediately.
                                             2 = good default for production.
                                             → "Most transient failures resolve in
                                               minutes. 2 retries covers network
                                               timeouts and brief DB locks."

retry_delay                   timedelta(0)   Wait time before first retry.
                                             timedelta(minutes=5) = good default.
                                             → "Give the system time to recover."

retry_exponential_backoff     False          If True: each retry waits longer.
                                             1st retry: 5min, 2nd: ~10min, 3rd: ~20min
                                             → "Useful for rate limits and cascading
                                               failures. Gives external systems
                                               progressively more recovery time."

max_retry_delay               None           Caps exponential backoff.
                                             timedelta(minutes=30) = good cap.
                                             Without this, backoff could grow to hours.

email_on_failure              True           Send email when task fails (after all
                                             retries exhausted). Set to True in prod.

email_on_retry                False          Send email on each retry attempt.
                                             ⚠️ Set to False — retries are expected.
                                             → "Alert fatigue. If I email on every
                                               retry, team ignores all alerts."

email                         []             List of email addresses for alerts.
                                             Must be quoted strings in a list.
                                             ❌ [team@x.com]
                                             ✅ ["team@x.com"]

execution_timeout             None           Max time a SINGLE TASK can run.
                                             If exceeded, task is killed.
                                             timedelta(hours=2) = safety net.
                                             → "Prevents zombie tasks that run forever
                                               due to a hung query or infinite loop."

sla                           None           Expected completion time for a task.
                                             If exceeded, Airflow logs an SLA miss
                                             and can trigger sla_miss_callback.
                                             Does NOT kill the task — just alerts.
                                             → "SLA is a monitoring tool, not a kill
                                               switch. execution_timeout kills."

on_failure_callback           None           Python function called when task fails.
                                             Common: send Slack alert, log to DB.
                                             def notify_slack(context):
                                                 send_slack(context['task_instance'])

on_success_callback           None           Python function called on success.
                                             Less common. Used for audit logging.

on_retry_callback             None           Python function called on each retry.
                                             Useful for logging retry attempts.

pool                          "default_pool" Worker pool this task runs in.
                                             Pools limit concurrent tasks.
                                             → "I use pools to limit DB connections.
                                               E.g., 'snowflake_pool' with 10 slots
                                               prevents overwhelming Snowflake."

priority_weight               1              Higher = runs first when queued.
                                             Useful for critical tasks.

queue                         "default"      Which Celery queue to use.
                                             → "Route heavy tasks to beefy workers,
                                               light tasks to small workers."

trigger_rule                  "all_success"  When this task runs relative to parents.
                                             (see section 5 below for all rules)


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2. @dag() ARGUMENTS — the DAG definition itself
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

@dag(
    dag_id="claims_daily_pipeline",
    default_args=DEFAULT_ARGS,
    description="Daily claims pipeline",
    schedule="0 6 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    max_active_runs=1,
    max_active_tasks=16,
    dagrun_timeout=timedelta(hours=6),
    tags=["claims", "production"],
    doc_md="## Claims Pipeline\nProcesses daily claims.",
    render_template_as_native_obj=True,
)

PARAMETER                       DEFAULT        EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

dag_id                          (required)     Unique identifier. Shows in Airflow UI.
                                               Must be unique across ALL DAGs.
                                               Convention: snake_case, descriptive.

default_args                    {}             Dict applied to all tasks (see section 1).

description                     ""             Shows in Airflow UI next to dag_id.
                                               Short summary for teammates.

schedule                        None           When to run. Accepts:
                                               - Cron string: "0 6 * * *"
                                               - timedelta: timedelta(hours=2)
                                               - Timetable object (custom schedules)
                                               - Dataset trigger (Airflow 2.4+)
                                               - None = manual trigger only

start_date                      (required)     Earliest date Airflow generates runs for.
                                               ⚠️ Use datetime(), NOT timedelta()!
                                               Combined with catchup=False, means:
                                               "only run from deployment forward."
                                               → Interview trap: "What happens if
                                                 start_date is last year and catchup
                                                 is True?" → backfill storm.

end_date                        None           Stop generating runs after this date.
                                               Rarely used. For temporary/one-off DAGs.

catchup                         True           ⚠️ CRITICAL — set to False in production.
                                               If True + start_date in the past:
                                               Airflow creates runs for EVERY missed
                                               interval since start_date.
                                               → "catchup=False means only run from now.
                                                 For historical backfill, I trigger
                                                 manually with controlled parallelism."

max_active_runs                 conf value     Max concurrent DAG runs.
                                               1 = one at a time (prevents overlap).
                                               → "If today's run is slow and tomorrow's
                                                 starts, they'd write to the same table.
                                                 max_active_runs=1 prevents that."

max_active_tasks                conf value     Max tasks running simultaneously WITHIN
                                               a single DAG run. Limits parallelism.
                                               16 = reasonable default.
                                               → "Controls resource usage. If I have
                                                 100 tasks that fan out, I don't want
                                                 all 100 hitting Snowflake at once."

dagrun_timeout                  None           Max time for an ENTIRE DAG run.
                                               If exceeded, the run is marked failed.
                                               timedelta(hours=6) = good safety net.
                                               → "Different from execution_timeout:
                                                 that's per-task, this is per-run."

tags                            []             Labels for UI filtering/search.
                                               ❌ task: ["etl"]  (your old typo)
                                               ✅ tags=["etl", "production"]

doc_md                          None           Markdown documentation shown in UI.
                                               Good for runbooks and on-call info.

render_template_as_native_obj   False          If True: Jinja renders Python objects
                                               (dicts, lists) instead of strings.
                                               Useful with TaskFlow when passing
                                               complex XCom data in templates.

is_paused_upon_creation         True           New DAG starts paused in UI.
                                               Must manually unpause to run.
                                               → "Safety: new DAGs don't auto-run
                                                 until someone reviews and unpauses."

concurrency (deprecated)        —              Use max_active_tasks instead.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3. S3KeySensor ARGUMENTS — waiting for files in S3
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

wait_file = S3KeySensor(
    task_id="wait_claims_file",
    bucket_name="insurance-landing",
    bucket_key="claims/{{ ds }}/claims.json",
    aws_conn_id="aws_default",
    poke_interval=300,
    timeout=14400,
    deferrable=True,
    wildcard_match=False,
)

PARAMETER                DEFAULT        EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

task_id                  (required)     Unique name within this DAG.
                                        Shows in UI and logs.

bucket_name              (required)     S3 bucket to check.
                                        Just the name, no "s3://" prefix.

bucket_key               (required)     Path inside bucket.
                                        Supports Jinja: {{ ds }}, {{ ts }}.
                                        Can use wildcards if wildcard_match=True.
                                        Example: "data/{{ ds }}/*.parquet"

aws_conn_id              "aws_default"  Airflow connection with AWS credentials.
                                        Never hardcode access keys.

poke_interval            60             Seconds between each check.
                                        300 (5 min) = good for daily pipelines.
                                        60 (1 min) = for time-sensitive data.
                                        → "Balance: too frequent = wasted API calls,
                                          too slow = added latency."

timeout                  604800 (7d)    Seconds before giving up.
                                        14400 (4 hours) = good for daily files.
                                        If exceeded: task fails → triggers alerts.
                                        → "If the file doesn't arrive in 4 hours,
                                          something is wrong upstream."

mode                     "poke"         How the sensor waits:
                                        ⚠️ See SENSOR MODES section below.

deferrable               False          ⚠️ THE MODERN WAY (Airflow 2.6+).
                                        True = hands off to async Triggerer.
                                        ZERO worker slots used while waiting.
                                        → "On Astronomer, deferrable=True is the
                                          recommended pattern. Even better than
                                          reschedule because it uses zero workers."

soft_fail                False          If True: timeout marks task as SKIPPED
                                        instead of FAILED. Downstream skipped too.
                                        → "Use when missing data is acceptable
                                          and you don't want it to fail the DAG."

exponential_backoff      False          Increase poke_interval between checks.
                                        Good for long waits (overnight files).

wildcard_match           False          If True: bucket_key supports wildcards.
                                        "data/{{ ds }}/*.parquet" matches any
                                        parquet file in that prefix.

SENSOR MODES — know the evolution:

  mode="poke" (OLD — avoid in production)
  ├── Checks every poke_interval seconds
  ├── HOLDS a worker slot the ENTIRE time
  └── 100 sensors = 100 blocked workers = no capacity for real tasks

  mode="reschedule" (BETTER)
  ├── Checks, then RELEASES worker slot
  ├── Re-claims a worker for each check
  ├── Worker is free between checks
  └── Still uses a worker briefly on each poke

  deferrable=True (BEST — Airflow 2.6+)
  ├── Hands off to Triggerer (separate async process)
  ├── ZERO worker slots used while waiting
  ├── Triggerer handles thousands of sensors efficiently
  ├── When condition met → Triggerer wakes up the task
  └── Astronomer recommended pattern

  Interview answer:
  "I use deferrable=True because it offloads the waiting to Airflow's
   async Triggerer process, using zero worker slots. On Astronomer,
   this is the recommended approach. It's the evolution from poke
   (blocks worker) → reschedule (releases between checks) → deferrable
   (never uses a worker while waiting)."


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
4. ExternalTaskSensor ARGUMENTS — waiting for another DAG
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

wait_upstream = ExternalTaskSensor(
    task_id="wait_upstream_dag",
    external_dag_id="reference_data_refresh",
    external_task_id="load_complete",
    allowed_states=["success"],
    execution_delta=timedelta(hours=1),
    timeout=3600,
    deferrable=True,
    poke_interval=60,
)

PARAMETER                DEFAULT             EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

external_dag_id          (required)          dag_id of the DAG you're waiting for.

external_task_id         None                Specific task in that DAG.
                                             None = wait for entire DAG to complete.
                                             "final_task" = wait for that specific task.

allowed_states           ["success"]         Which states count as "done."
                                             ["success"] = only if it succeeded.
                                             ["success", "skipped"] = also OK if skipped.

execution_delta          None                Time offset between DAG schedules.
                                             If upstream runs at 5 AM and yours at 6 AM:
                                             execution_delta=timedelta(hours=1)
                                             → "Look for the run that started 1h before
                                               mine."

execution_date_fn        None                Alternative to execution_delta.
                                             Python function that returns the target
                                             execution date. More flexible.

check_existence          False               If True: also verify the external DAG/task
                                             actually exists. Fails early if mistyped.

timeout                  604800 (7d)         Same as S3KeySensor.

deferrable               False               Same as S3KeySensor. Use True.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
5. TRIGGER RULES — when a task runs relative to upstream
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule

RULE                              RUNS WHEN
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ALL_SUCCESS (default)             ALL upstream tasks succeeded.
                                  → Normal tasks, happy path.

ALL_FAILED                        ALL upstream tasks failed.
                                  → Rare. "Only run if everything broke."

ALL_DONE                          ALL upstream tasks finished (any status).
                                  → Cleanup tasks: delete temp files, release
                                    resources. Must always run.

ONE_SUCCESS                       At least ONE upstream succeeded.
                                  → "Run if any branch worked."

ONE_FAILED                        At least ONE upstream failed.
                                  → Failure notifications. EmailOperator.
                                  → "Send alert the moment anything breaks."

ONE_DONE                          At least ONE upstream finished.
                                  → Quick reactions.

NONE_FAILED                       No upstream FAILED (success or skipped OK).
                                  → "Run unless something crashed."

NONE_FAILED_MIN_ONE_SUCCESS       No upstream failed AND at least one succeeded.
                                  → End-of-DAG markers. EmptyOperator("end").
                                  → "Final checkpoint: nothing broke and
                                    something actually ran."

NONE_SKIPPED                      No upstream was skipped.
                                  → "Run only if all branches executed."

ALWAYS                            Always runs, regardless of upstream.
                                  → Monitoring/logging tasks.

Interview pattern — know these 4:
  ALL_SUCCESS    → normal tasks (default)
  ONE_FAILED     → failure email alerts
  ALL_DONE       → cleanup (always runs)
  NONE_FAILED_MIN_ONE_SUCCESS → end marker


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
6. @task() ARGUMENTS — TaskFlow API task decorator
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

@task(
    task_id="validate_source",
    retries=3,
    retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=10),
    execution_timeout=timedelta(hours=1),
    pool="snowflake_pool",
    trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_SUCCESS,
    multiple_outputs=False,
)
def validate_source(ds: str = None) -> dict:
    ...

PARAMETER                DEFAULT           EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

task_id                  function name     Auto-generated from function name.
                                           Can override explicitly.

retries                  from default_args Per-task override.
                                           → "This task talks to flaky API,
                                             so I give it 3 retries instead of 2."

retry_delay              from default_args Per-task override.

execution_timeout        from default_args Per-task max runtime. Kills if exceeded.

pool                     "default_pool"    Worker pool. Limits concurrency.
                                           → "I put all Snowflake tasks in
                                             'snowflake_pool' to limit connections."

trigger_rule             ALL_SUCCESS       When this task runs (see section 5).

multiple_outputs         False             If True: return dict is split into
                                           separate XCom entries per key.
                                           False = entire dict is one XCom entry.
                                           Usually leave False.

SPECIAL PARAMETERS auto-injected by Airflow (add to function signature):

  ds: str           → execution date as string "2026-06-09"
  ts: str           → execution timestamp "2026-06-09T06:00:00+00:00"
  run_id: str       → unique run identifier
  data_interval_start  → start of data interval (pendulum DateTime)
  data_interval_end    → end of data interval (pendulum DateTime)
  **kwargs          → catch-all for all context variables

  → "ds is the most common. Airflow injects it automatically if I name
    the parameter 'ds'. No manual XCom pull needed."


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
7. EmailOperator ARGUMENTS — notifications
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

notify = EmailOperator(
    task_id="notify_success",
    to=["team@company.com"],
    cc=["manager@company.com"],
    subject="Pipeline {{ ds }} — SUCCESS",
    html_content="<p>Done. Rows: {{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='qc')['row_count'] }}</p>",
    trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_SUCCESS,
)

PARAMETER         EXPLANATION
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

to                List of recipient emails. Must be list, not string.
cc                Carbon copy list.
subject           Email subject. Supports Jinja: {{ ds }}, {{ ts }}.
html_content      Email body in HTML. Supports Jinja.
                  ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='X') fetches XCom from task X.
trigger_rule      Typically:
                  ALL_SUCCESS for success emails.
                  ONE_FAILED for failure emails.


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
8. HOOK METHODS — S3Hook, SnowflakeHook, PostgresHook
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

S3Hook(aws_conn_id="aws_default")
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  .head_object(key, bucket_name)  → metadata dict (size, date, type)
                                    No download. Cheap. Use for validation.
  .list_keys(bucket_name, prefix) → list of S3 key strings
                                    Check output file count.
  .read_key(key, bucket_name)     → file content as string
                                    Small files only (JSON, CSV).
  .load_string(string, key, bucket_name)  → upload string to S3
  .check_for_key(key, bucket_name)        → True/False, file exists?

SnowflakeHook(snowflake_conn_id="snowflake_default")
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  .run(sql)                       → execute SQL (MERGE, INSERT, DDL)
                                    No return value. For write operations.
  .get_first(sql)                 → first row as tuple. (count,) or None.
                                    Use for: SELECT COUNT(*), single values.
  .get_records(sql)               → all rows as list of tuples.
                                    Use for: small result sets.
  .get_pandas_df(sql)             → pandas DataFrame.
                                    Use for: analysis, small-medium data.

PostgresHook(postgres_conn_id="postgres_prod")
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  .run(sql)                       → same as Snowflake
  .get_first(sql)                 → same
  .get_records(sql)               → same
  .get_pandas_df(sql)             → same
  .copy_expert(sql, file)         → COPY command for bulk loads


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
9. JINJA TEMPLATES — variables available in templates
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Used in: bucket_key, sql parameters, email subject/body, Operator args.
NOT in: @task function code (use the ds parameter instead).

VARIABLE                 EXAMPLE VALUE                  USE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
{{ ds }}                 "2026-06-09"                   execution date
{{ ds_nodash }}          "20260609"                     date without dashes
{{ ts }}                 "2026-06-09T06:00:00+00:00"    full timestamp
{{ execution_date }}     DateTime object                pendulum datetime
{{ data_interval_start}} DateTime object                interval start
{{ data_interval_end }}  DateTime object                interval end
{{ prev_ds }}            "2026-06-08"                   previous date
{{ next_ds }}            "2026-06-10"                   next date
{{ run_id }}             "scheduled__2026-..."          unique run ID
{{ dag.dag_id }}         "claims_daily_pipeline"        DAG name
{{ task.task_id }}       "validate_source"              task name
{{ var.value.key }}      (from Variable)                Airflow Variable
{{ conn.conn_id.host }}  (from Connection)              Connection field

XCom in templates:
{{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='quality_check')['row_count'] }}
→ Pulls XCom from task 'quality_check', gets 'row_count' key.

Date math:
{{ macros.ds_add(ds, -1) }}      → yesterday
{{ macros.ds_add(ds, 7) }}       → 7 days later
{{ macros.ds_format(ds, ...) }}  → custom format


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
10. CRON SCHEDULE — quick reference
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Format:  MIN  HOUR  DAY  MONTH  WEEKDAY
          │    │     │     │      │
          │    │     │     │      └─ 0=Sun, 1=Mon, ..., 6=Sat
          │    │     │     └──────── 1-12
          │    │     └────────────── 1-31
          │    └──────────────────── 0-23
          └───────────────────────── 0-59

"0 6 * * *"        Daily at 6 AM
"0 */2 * * *"      Every 2 hours
"0 6 * * 1"        Every Monday at 6 AM
"0 6 1 * *"        First of month at 6 AM
"30 8 * * 1-5"     Weekdays at 8:30 AM
"0 0 * * 0"        Sunday at midnight
"*/15 * * * *"     Every 15 minutes
None               Manual trigger only


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
11. EXECUTION DATE LOGIC — the #1 interview trap
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Airflow runs at the END of the data interval.

  DAG schedule: daily at 6 AM
  Run fires:    June 10 at 6:00 AM
  ds =          "2026-06-09"     ← YESTERDAY

  data_interval_start = June 9, 06:00
  data_interval_end   = June 10, 06:00

  Logic: "Data for June 9th is ready by June 10th morning → process it."

  {{ ds }} already gives you yesterday. No {{ ds - 1 }} needed.

  When you WOULD offset:
  - DAG runs Monday, need Friday's data: macros.ds_add(ds, -3)
  - DAG runs at noon, need morning file: use data_interval_start


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
12. AIRFLOW VARIABLES — runtime config
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

from airflow.models import Variable

⚠️ ALWAYS inside @task functions, NEVER at module level.
  Module level = runs on every scheduler parse (~30s) = slow + breaks.

Variable.get("key")                          → returns string value
Variable.get("key", default_var="fallback")  → with fallback
Variable.get("json_key", deserialize_json=True)  → returns dict/list
Variable.set("key", "value")                 → set from code

In Jinja templates:
  {{ var.value.bucket_name }}      → string variable
  {{ var.json.config.key }}        → JSON variable, specific key


━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
13. EXECUTORS — how tasks run (interview topic)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

EXECUTOR             DESCRIPTION                         USE CASE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SequentialExecutor   One task at a time, same process.   Dev/testing only.
LocalExecutor        Parallel, single machine.           Small/medium prod.
CeleryExecutor       Distributed workers via message     Large production.
                     broker (Redis/RabbitMQ).
KubernetesExecutor   Each task = K8s pod.                Production on K8s.
                     Isolated resources per task.        Astronomer uses this.

"On Astronomer, it's typically KubernetesExecutor or CeleryExecutor.
 Astronomer manages the infrastructure — I focus on DAG code."

cards.title: Imports
cards.prompt: **Imports** — write it from memory.
cards.answer:
# === AIRFLOW IMPORTS ===

# Core — datetime for scheduling, decorators for the modern TaskFlow API
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow.decorators import dag, task

# Sensors — these are operators that WAIT for a condition before proceeding.
# S3KeySensor waits for a file to land in S3,
# ExternalTaskSensor waits for a task in another DAG to finish.
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor
from airflow.sensors.external_task import ExternalTaskSensor

# Hooks — these give us a programmatic connection to external systems.
# Think of hooks as the low-level client wrappers: they manage auth
# and expose helper methods to interact with S3, Postgres, Snowflake, etc.
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.hooks.s3 import S3Hook
from airflow.providers.postgres.hooks.postgres import PostgresHook
from airflow.providers.snowflake.hooks.snowflake import SnowflakeHook

# Operators — units of work. EmailOperator sends emails,
# PythonOperator runs a Python callable, EmptyOperator is a no-op placeholder
# useful as a join point or marker in the DAG graph.
from airflow.operators.email import EmailOperator
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from airflow.operators.empty import EmptyOperator

# Utils — TriggerRule controls WHEN a task runs relative to upstream status
# (e.g., run on failure for alerts). Variable lets us fetch key-value config

cards.title: @task + XCom
cards.prompt:
**@task + XCom** — write it from memory.

"With TaskFlow API, I define tasks as Python functions decorated with @task.
 The return value is automatically pushed to XCom, and when I pass it as
 an argument to another task, Airflow auto-pulls it — no manual XCom calls needed."
cards.answer:
# === TASK DECORATOR ===
# "With TaskFlow API, I define tasks as Python functions decorated with @task.
#  The return value is automatically pushed to XCom, and when I pass it as
#  an argument to another task, Airflow auto-pulls it — no manual XCom calls needed."

# Basic task — receives the execution date (ds) as a string like "2025-06-01"
# Airflow auto-injects 'ds' if I name the parameter that way.
@task()
def extract(ds: str = None) -> dict:
    """ds = execution date, auto-injected by Airflow."""
    # "I return a dict — Airflow serializes this to XCom automatically,
    #  and downstream tasks can consume it as a function argument."
    return {"path": f"s3://bucket/{ds}/", "date": ds}


# Task with multiple inputs — receives dicts from two different upstream tasks.
# This is useful for aggregation or cross-validation between pipeline stages.
@task()
def quality_check(silver_info: dict, gold_info: dict) -> dict:
    # "I check for zero records as a data quality gate — fail fast
    #  before bad data propagates downstream."
    if gold_info["records"] == 0:
        raise ValueError("ZERO records in Gold!")
    return {"status": "passed"}


# Wiring (inside DAG function) — this is how TaskFlow tasks connect.
# "I call the task functions and pass return values as arguments.
#  Airflow interprets this as: 'run extract first, then transform,
#  and pass the XCom output between them automatically.'"
extracted = extract()
transformed = transform(extracted)       # data flows via XCom
qc = quality_check(silver, gold)         # multiple inputs

cards.title: subprocess + spark-submit
cards.prompt:
**subprocess + spark-submit** — write it from memory.

"When Airflow orchestrates Spark jobs, one common approach is shelling out
 to spark-submit via subprocess. The Airflow task just launches and monitors
 the Spark job — the heavy processing happens on the Spark cluster."
cards.answer:
# === SUBPROCESS — SPARK SUBMIT ===
# "When Airflow orchestrates Spark jobs, one common approach is shelling out
#  to spark-submit via subprocess. The Airflow task just launches and monitors
#  the Spark job — the heavy processing happens on the Spark cluster."

import subprocess
import json

def run_spark_job(script_name: str, args: list = None) -> dict:
    """Reusable: submit Spark job, return metadata."""

    # "I build the spark-submit command as a list — safer than string concatenation,
    #  avoids shell injection, and handles spaces in arguments."
    cmd = [
        "spark-submit",
        "--master", "yarn",             # submit to YARN cluster (could also be k8s, standalone)
        "--deploy-mode", "client",      # driver runs on Airflow worker; 'cluster' runs driver on YARN
        "--conf", "spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200",  # tune parallelism for shuffle-heavy ops
        "--conf", "spark.executor.memory=4g",          # memory per executor
        f"/opt/airflow/scripts/{script_name}",         # path to the PySpark script
    ] + (args or [])  # append any extra arguments (e.g., dates, paths)

    # "subprocess.run blocks until Spark finishes. capture_output=True catches
    #  stdout/stderr for logging. timeout prevents zombie jobs running forever."
    proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=7200)

    # "If Spark exits non-zero, the job failed. I raise an error with the last
    #  2000 chars of stderr — enough for the error message without flooding logs."
    if proc.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Spark failed (exit {proc.returncode}): {proc.stderr[-2000:]}")

    # "My convention: the Spark script prints a JSON summary on its last line
    #  (record counts, output paths, etc.). I parse it from stdout so downstream
    #  tasks can use the metadata. I scan from the bottom to skip Spark's log noise."
    for line in reversed(proc.stdout.strip().split("\n")):
        try:
            return json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue

    # Fallback if no JSON found — at least we know it succeeded
    return {"status": "success"}

cards.title: Validate source
cards.prompt:
**Validate source** — write it from memory.

"This is a guard task — it runs BEFORE the heavy Spark job.
 The idea is fail fast: if the source file is missing or corrupt,
 we skip the expensive processing and save compute cost."
cards.answer:
# === VALIDATE SOURCE (before expensive processing) ===
# "This is a guard task — it runs BEFORE the heavy Spark job.
#  The idea is fail fast: if the source file is missing or corrupt,
#  we skip the expensive processing and save compute cost."

from tomlkit import datetime


@task()
def validate_source(ds: str = None) -> dict:
    """Check source file exists and has valid size. Fail fast = save money."""

    # "I use S3Hook to check the file without downloading it.
    #  head_object is an S3 API call that returns metadata only."
    hook = S3Hook(aws_conn_id="aws_default")
    key = f"data/daily/{ds}/raw.csv"

    # head_object returns file metadata — size, content type, last modified.
    # If the file doesn't exist, it throws an exception, which fails the task.
    metadata = hook.head_object(key=key, bucket_name="raw-bucket")
    size_mb = metadata["ContentLength"] / (1024 * 1024)

    # If not have modify the taks will not run
    if metadata["LastModified"].date() != datetime.strptime(ds, "%Y-%m-%d").date():
        raise ValueError(f"File last modified on {metadata['LastModified']} — expected {ds}")
    
    # "I check both too-small and too-large files.
    #  Too small (< 1 KB) usually means an empty or corrupt upload.
    #  Too large (> 5 GB) is suspicious and might indicate a duplicate or wrong file."
    if size_mb < 0.001:
        raise ValueError(f"File too small: {size_mb:.4f} MB — likely empty")
    if size_mb > 5000:
        raise ValueError(f"File too large: {size_mb:.1f} MB — investigate")

    # "I return a dict with the validated file info. Downstream tasks receive
    #  this via XCom and know the source is safe to process."
    return {
        "source_path": f"s3://raw-bucket/{key}",
        "size_mb": round(size_mb, 2),
        "date": ds,
    }

cards.title: Quality check
cards.prompt:
**Quality check** — write it from memory.

"This runs AFTER processing to validate the output.
 It's the other half of the validation sandwich: validate_source guards
 the input, quality_check guards the output."
cards.answer:
# === QUALITY CHECK (after processing) ===
# "This runs AFTER processing to validate the output.
#  It's the other half of the validation sandwich: validate_source guards
#  the input, quality_check guards the output."

@task()
def quality_check(process_info: dict) -> dict:
    """Validate output after processing."""

    # "First, I check that the Spark job actually wrote output files to S3.
    #  list_keys returns all files under the output prefix."
    hook = S3Hook(aws_conn_id="aws_default")
    keys = hook.list_keys(bucket_name="processed-bucket", prefix=process_info["output_path"])
    file_count = len(keys) if keys else 0

    # "Zero files means the job ran but produced nothing — a silent failure.
    #  This is worse than a crash because it looks successful in the logs."
    if file_count == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"No output files at {process_info['output_path']}")

    # "Second check: verify the data actually loaded into the database.
    #  I use PostgresHook to count rows in the target table."
    pg_hook = PostgresHook(postgres_conn_id="postgres_prod")
    result = pg_hook.get_first("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM target_table")
    row_count = result[0] if result else 0

    # "Zero rows after processing = something broke in the load step.
    #  Better to catch it here than discover it when a report is empty."
    if row_count == 0:
        raise ValueError("ZERO rows after processing!")

    # "I return the metrics so downstream tasks (like email notifications)
    #  can include them in success messages."
    return {"status": "passed", "file_count": file_count, "row_count": row_count}

cards.title: Wiring patterns
cards.prompt:
**Wiring patterns** — write it from memory.

"This is how we define task dependencies — the execution order.
 Airflow gives us two styles: bitshift operators and function-call chaining."
cards.answer:
# === WIRING PATTERNS ===
# "This is how we define task dependencies — the execution order.
#  Airflow gives us two styles: bitshift operators and function-call chaining."

# Sequential — >> means 'runs before'. Read left to right.
# "extract runs first, then transform, then load."
extract >> transform >> load

# Parallel sensors before a task — list syntax means both run in parallel,
# and validate_source only starts when BOTH sensors succeed.
# "I'm saying: wait for the file AND wait for the upstream DAG,
#  then once both are done, proceed with validation."
[wait_file, wait_upstream] >> validate_source

# "After transform completes, both quality checks run simultaneously."

# Fan-in — multiple tasks must all complete before the next one runs.
# "Both QC tasks must finish before we send notifications."
[qc_silver, qc_gold] >> notify_success
[qc_silver, qc_gold] >> notify_failure

# Decorator tasks — with TaskFlow API, dependencies are implicit via function calls.
# "When I pass the return value of one task as an argument to another,
#  Airflow automatically creates the dependency AND handles XCom transfer."
source = validate_source()
bronze = process_bronze(source)        # source dict passed via XCom
silver = transform_silver(bronze)      # bronze dict passed via XCom
gold = aggregate_gold(silver)

cards.title: TriggerRule
cards.prompt:
**TriggerRule** — write it from memory.

"Trigger rules control WHEN a task runs based on the status of its upstream tasks.
 By default, a task only runs if all parents succeeded. But sometimes we want
 different behavior — like running a cleanup task no matter what, or sending
 an alert only when something fails."
cards.answer:
# === TRIGGER RULES ===
# "Trigger rules control WHEN a task runs based on the status of its upstream tasks.
#  By default, a task only runs if all parents succeeded. But sometimes we want
#  different behavior — like running a cleanup task no matter what, or sending
#  an alert only when something fails."

from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule

# ALL_SUCCESS (default) — runs only if ALL upstream tasks succeeded.
# "This is what you get by default, no need to set it explicitly,
#  but I'm showing it here for completeness."
task_a = MyOperator(trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_SUCCESS)

# ONE_FAILED — runs if ANY upstream task failed.
# "Perfect for failure alerts: I wire this to an EmailOperator so the team
#  gets notified the moment anything goes wrong, even if other branches succeed."
notify_fail = EmailOperator(trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED)

# NONE_FAILED_MIN_ONE_SUCCESS — runs if NO upstream failed AND at least one succeeded.
# "This is useful for a final 'end' marker task. It handles cases where some
#  upstream tasks were skipped (not failed) — it still runs as long as nothing crashed."
final = EmptyOperator(task_id="end", trigger_rule=TriggerRule.NONE_FAILED_MIN_ONE_SUCCESS)

# ALL_DONE — runs regardless of upstream status (success, failed, or skipped).
# "I use this for cleanup tasks — like deleting temp files or releasing resources.
#  Cleanup must always run, even after failures."
cleanup = MyOperator(trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_DONE)

cards.title: Variable.get()
cards.prompt:
**Variable.get()** — write it from memory.

"Airflow Variables are key-value pairs stored in the metadata database.
 They let us externalize config (bucket names, environment flags, thresholds)
 without hardcoding them in the DAG file."
cards.answer:
# === AIRFLOW VARIABLES ===
# "Airflow Variables are key-value pairs stored in the metadata database.
#  They let us externalize config (bucket names, environment flags, thresholds)
#  without hardcoding them in the DAG file."

# IMPORTANT: Always call Variable.get() INSIDE functions, NOT at module level.
# "This is a common gotcha. Code at module level runs every time the scheduler
#  parses the DAG file — which happens every 30 seconds by default.
#  If Variable.get() is at module level, it hits the database on EVERY parse,
#  which slows down the scheduler and breaks if the variable doesn't exist yet."

from airflow.models import Variable

# WRONG — runs at parse time:
# "This line executes when the file is imported, not when the task runs.
#  It makes the scheduler slower and creates a hard dependency on the variable existing."
# bucket = Variable.get("raw_bucket")

# CORRECT — runs at execution time:
# "Inside a @task function, Variable.get() only runs when the task actually executes.
#  I also use default_var as a fallback so the DAG doesn't break in dev environments
#  where the variable might not be configured yet."
@task()
def my_task():
    bucket = Variable.get("raw_bucket", default_var="default-bucket")
    env = Variable.get("environment", default_var="dev")
    return {"bucket": bucket, "env": env}

""" FULL DAG TEMPLATE — Copy and customize. "This is a complete, production-ready DAG that ties together all the patterns we've seen: sensors, validation, processing, quality checks, and notifications." """ # --- IMPORTS --- # "Standard set: datetime for scheduling, decorators for TaskFlow API, # sensors to wait for external conditions, hooks to interact with services, # EmailOperator for alerts, TriggerRule for conditional execution." from datetime import datetime, timedelta from airflow.decorators import dag, task from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.hooks.s3 import S3Hook from airflow.providers.postgres.hooks.postgres import PostgresHook from airflow.sensors.external_task import ExternalTaskSensor from airflow.operators.email import EmailOperator from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule import subprocess import json # --- DEFAULT ARGS --- # "Applied to every task in the DAG — retry policy, alerting, ownership." DEFAULT_ARGS = { "owner": "data-engineering", "depends_on_past": False, "retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5), "email_on_failure": True, "email": ["team@company.com"], } # --- DAG DEFINITION --- # "I decorate the function with @dag. Everything inside becomes the DAG's scope." @dag( dag_id="daily_pipeline", default_args=DEFAULT_ARGS, schedule="0 6 * * *", # runs every day at 6 AM UTC start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1), catchup=False, # don't backfill historical runs max_active_runs=1, # prevent overlapping runs tags=["etl", "production"], ) def daily_pipeline(): # --- SENSOR: Wait for source file --- # "First thing in the DAG: a sensor that blocks until the input file # lands in S3. Nothing downstream runs until this succeeds." wait_file = S3KeySensor( task_id="wait_file", bucket_name="raw-bucket", bucket_key="data/{{ ds }}/input.csv", # {{ ds }} = execution date aws_conn_id="aws_default", poke_interval=300, # poll every 5 min timeout=14400, # fail after 4 hours mode="reschedule", # release worker between checks ) # --- TASK: Validate source file --- # "Guard task — checks the file exists and has a sane size before # we spend compute on processing." @task() def validate(ds: str = None) -> dict: hook = S3Hook(aws_conn_id="aws_default") meta = hook.head_object(key=f"data/{ds}/input.csv", bucket_name="raw-bucket") size_mb = meta["ContentLength"] / (1024 * 1024) if size_mb < 0.001: raise ValueError(f"File too small: {size_mb:.4f} MB") return {"path": f"s3://raw-bucket/data/{ds}/input.csv", "size_mb": round(size_mb, 2), "date": ds} # --- TASK: Process data --- # "Main processing step — in production this would call spark-submit # or run transformation logic. Takes the validated source info as input." @task() def process(source: dict) -> dict: # subprocess.run spark-submit or transformation logic return {"output": f"s3://processed/{source['date']}/", "records": 5000} # --- TASK: Quality check --- # "Post-processing validation — ensures we actually produced data. # Zero records = silent failure, which is worse than a crash." @task() def quality_check(result: dict) -> dict: if result["records"] == 0: raise ValueError("ZERO records!") return {"status": "passed", "records": result["records"]} # --- NOTIFICATIONS --- # "Two email tasks with different trigger rules: # success email only fires if everything passed, # failure email fires if anything failed." notify_ok = EmailOperator( task_id="notify_success", to=["team@company.com"], subject="Pipeline {{ ds }} SUCCESS", # ti.xcom_pull grabs the quality_check output to include record count in email html_content="

Done. Records: {{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='quality_check')['records'] }}

", trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_SUCCESS, ) notify_fail = EmailOperator( task_id="notify_failure", to=["team@company.com"], subject="Pipeline {{ ds }} FAILED", html_content="

Failed. Check logs.

", trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED, # runs when ANY upstream fails ) # --- WIRING --- # "This is the execution graph — read it top to bottom: # 1. Wait for file to arrive in S3 # 2. Validate the file (size check) # 3. Process the data # 4. Run quality check # 5. Send success OR failure email based on outcome" source = validate() wait_file >> source # sensor must pass before validation result = process(source) # XCom carries validated source info to process qc = quality_check(result) # XCom carries process output to QC qc >> notify_ok # success email only if QC passed qc >> notify_fail # failure email only if QC (or anything upstream) failed # "Final line: instantiate the DAG so Airflow's scheduler discovers it." daily_pipeline()

cards.title: DAG factory (config-driven)
cards.prompt: Reference — DAG factory (config-driven)
cards.answer:
""" ============================================================================ DAG FACTORY — Python script that generates DAGs from YAML config ============================================================================ "This is the factory script. It reads the YAML config file and generates one DAG per entry. The pattern is: loop through config → for each pipeline, create a DAG with the right sensor, tasks, quality checks, and notifications. The key insight is: the YAML defines WHAT (source, destination, schedule), and this script defines HOW (which operators, which hooks, which wiring). New pipelines = new YAML entry. No changes to this file." HOW IT WORKS: 1. Script reads pipelines.yaml at parse time 2. For each pipeline entry, it calls create_dag() 3. create_dag() builds a complete DAG with: sensor → validate → process → QC → notify 4. Each generated DAG is registered in globals() so Airflow discovers it FILE STRUCTURE: dags/ ├── dag_factory.py ← THIS FILE (Airflow parses it) └── config/ └── pipelines.yaml ← pipeline definitions """ from datetime import datetime, timedelta from pathlib import Path import yaml from airflow.decorators import dag, task from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.hooks.s3 import S3Hook from airflow.operators.email import EmailOperator from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule # ── Step 1: Load YAML config ─────────────────────────────────────────────── # "I read the config at module level because Airflow needs to discover # DAGs at parse time. This is one of the few things that SHOULD run # at module level — unlike Variable.get() which should be inside tasks." CONFIG_PATH = Path(__file__).parent / "config" / "pipelines.yaml" with open(CONFIG_PATH, "r") as f: pipelines_config = yaml.safe_load(f) # ── Step 2: DAG creation function ────────────────────────────────────────── # "This function takes one pipeline config dict and returns a fully # wired DAG. I call it once per pipeline entry in the YAML." def create_dag(pipeline_id: str, config: dict): """Generate a complete DAG from a config dictionary.""" # Build default_args from config default_args = { "owner": config.get("owner", "data-engineering"), "depends_on_past": False, "retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5), "email_on_failure": config.get("notifications", {}).get("on_failure", True), "email": config.get("notifications", {}).get("email", ["team@company.com"]), } # "I use the @dag decorator inside this function. The trick is: # each call creates a unique DAG with its own dag_id from the config." @dag( dag_id=pipeline_id, default_args=default_args, description=config.get("description", ""), schedule=config.get("schedule"), # None = manual trigger start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), catchup=False, max_active_runs=1, tags=config.get("tags", []), ) def generated_dag(): source_cfg = config["source"] processing_cfg = config["processing"] qc_cfg = config.get("quality_checks", {}) notify_cfg = config.get("notifications", {}) # ── SENSOR: Wait for source file ── # "The sensor is created based on source.type in the YAML. if source_cfg["type"] == "s3": wait_source = S3KeySensor( task_id="wait_source_file", bucket_name=source_cfg["bucket"], bucket_key=source_cfg["key_pattern"], # Jinja template aws_conn_id=source_cfg.get("conn_id", "aws_default"), poke_interval=300, timeout=14400, mode="reschedule", ) # ── TASK: Validate source ── # "Generic validation that works for any S3-based pipeline. # The thresholds come from the YAML config." @task() def validate_source(ds: str = None) -> dict: hook = S3Hook(aws_conn_id=source_cfg.get("conn_id", "aws_default")) # Resolve the Jinja-like pattern with the actual date key = source_cfg["key_pattern"].replace("{{ ds }}", ds) metadata = hook.head_object(key=key, bucket_name=source_cfg["bucket"]) size_mb = metadata["ContentLength"] / (1024 * 1024) max_size = qc_cfg.get("max_file_size_mb", 5000) if size_mb < 0.001: raise ValueError(f"[{pipeline_id}] File too small: {size_mb:.4f} MB") if size_mb > max_size: raise ValueError(f"[{pipeline_id}] File too large: {size_mb:.1f} MB") return { "source_path": f"s3://{source_cfg['bucket']}/{key}", "size_mb": round(size_mb, 2), "date": ds, "pipeline": pipeline_id, } # ── TASK: Process data ── # "The processing logic varies by type. For 'spark', I'd call # spark-submit. For 'python', I'd call a function directly." @task() def process_data(source_info: dict) -> dict: if processing_cfg["type"] == "spark": import subprocess, json spark_conf_args = [] for k, v in processing_cfg.get("spark_conf", {}).items(): spark_conf_args.extend(["--conf", f"{k}={v}"]) cmd = [ "spark-submit", "--master", "yarn", "--deploy-mode", "client", ] + spark_conf_args + [ f"/opt/airflow/scripts/{processing_cfg['script']}", "--date", source_info["date"], "--source", source_info["source_path"], ] proc = subprocess.run( cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=7200 ) if proc.returncode != 0: raise RuntimeError( f"[{pipeline_id}] Spark failed: {proc.stderr[-2000:]}" ) # Parse JSON metadata from last stdout line for line in reversed(proc.stdout.strip().split("\n")): try: return json.loads(line) except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError): continue # Fallback return { "status": "success", "date": source_info["date"], "pipeline": pipeline_id, "records": 0, } # ── TASK: Quality check ── @task() def quality_check(result: dict) -> dict: min_records = qc_cfg.get("min_records", 1) records = result.get("records", 0) if records < min_records: raise ValueError( f"[{pipeline_id}] Only {records} records — minimum is {min_records}" ) return { "status": "passed", "records": records, "pipeline": pipeline_id, } # ── NOTIFICATIONS ── email_list = notify_cfg.get("email", ["team@company.com"]) notify_ok = EmailOperator( task_id="notify_success", to=email_list, subject=f"{pipeline_id}" + " {{ ds }} — SUCCESS", html_content=f"

{pipeline_id} completed. " "Records: {{{{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='quality_check')['records'] }}}}

", trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ALL_SUCCESS, ) notify_fail = EmailOperator( task_id="notify_failure", to=email_list, subject=f"{pipeline_id}" + " {{ ds }} — FAILED", html_content=f"

{pipeline_id} failed. Check Airflow logs.

", trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED, ) # ── WIRING ── # "Same pattern as a hand-written DAG: # sensor → validate → process → quality check → notify" source = validate_source() wait_source >> source result = process_data(source) qc = quality_check(result) qc >> notify_ok qc >> notify_fail # Return the instantiated DAG return generated_dag() # ── Step 3: Generate all DAGs ────────────────────────────────────────────── # "This is the key part. I loop through every pipeline in the YAML # and register each generated DAG in globals(). Airflow scans globals() # of every file in the dags/ folder looking for DAG objects." for pipeline_id, pipeline_config in pipelines_config.items(): # globals()[pipeline_id] makes the DAG discoverable by Airflow globals()[pipeline_id] = create_dag(pipeline_id, pipeline_config) # ============================================================================ # INTERVIEW TALKING POINTS # ============================================================================ """ WHY THIS PATTERN: "Instead of writing 50 separate DAG files that are 90% identical, I write ONE factory script and a config file. Benefits: - New pipeline = add YAML block, zero Python changes - Consistent patterns across ALL pipelines (same retry, alerting, QC) - One place to upgrade behavior (fix factory = fix all DAGs) - Easier code review (reviewers check YAML, not boilerplate Python)" HOW AIRFLOW DISCOVERS GENERATED DAGS: "Airflow's scheduler scans every .py file in the dags/ folder. It looks for DAG objects in the module's globals(). When I do: globals()[pipeline_id] = create_dag(...) I'm adding a DAG object to this module's namespace, so Airflow finds it." TRADE-OFFS: "Not every pipeline fits the factory pattern. Complex one-off pipelines with unique branching or custom logic are better as hand-written DAGs. The factory works best when you have many similar pipelines — like 50 source-to-warehouse ingestion jobs that differ only in source/dest." SCALING: "If the YAML grows too large, I split it into multiple files: config/claims.yaml, config/policies.yaml, config/payments.yaml. The factory script reads all YAML files from the config/ directory." """

cards.title: DAG factory YAML config
cards.prompt: Reference — DAG factory YAML config
cards.answer:
# "I define all pipeline metadata in YAML because it separates WHAT the pipeline
#  does from HOW it runs. Non-developers can review and modify pipeline config.
#  The factory script is the HOW — it reads this config and builds DAGs."

# ── Pipeline 1: Daily insurance claims ──────────────────────────────────────
claims_daily:
  # dag_id is generated from the key name: "claims_daily"
  description: "Daily claims ingestion from S3 to Postgres"
  schedule: "0 6 * * *"           # 6 AM daily
  owner: "claims-team"
  tags: ["claims", "daily", "production"]

  # Source config — where data comes from
  source:
    type: "s3"                     # tells factory which sensor + hook to use
    bucket: "insurance-raw"
    key_pattern: "claims/{{ ds }}/claims.json"   # Jinja template for date
    conn_id: "aws_default"

  # Processing config
  processing:
    type: "spark"                  # tells factory to use spark-submit
    script: "process_claims.py"
    spark_conf:
      spark.executor.memory: "4g"
      spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "200"

  # Destination config — where data lands
  destination:
    type: "postgres"
    conn_id: "postgres_prod"
    table: "claims_processed"

  # Quality checks — what to validate after processing
  quality_checks:
    min_records: 100               # fail if fewer than 100 records
    max_file_size_mb: 5000         # fail if source file > 5 GB
    check_output_exists: true      # verify S3 output files exist

  # Alerting
  notifications:
    email: ["claims-team@company.com"]
    on_failure: true
    on_success: true


# ── Pipeline 2: Weekly policy summary ───────────────────────────────────────
# "Adding a new pipeline = adding a new block here. No Python changes."
policy_weekly:
  description: "Weekly policy aggregation"
  schedule: "0 8 * * 1"           # Monday at 8 AM
  owner: "policy-team"
  tags: ["policy", "weekly", "production"]

  source:
    type: "s3"
    bucket: "insurance-raw"
    key_pattern: "policies/{{ ds }}/policies.parquet"
    conn_id: "aws_default"

  processing:
    type: "spark"
    script: "aggregate_policies.py"
    spark_conf:
      spark.executor.memory: "8g"
      spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "400"

  destination:
    type: "snowflake"
    conn_id: "snowflake_default"
    table: "policy_summary"

  quality_checks:
    min_records: 50
    max_file_size_mb: 10000
    check_output_exists: true

  notifications:
    email: ["policy-team@company.com"]
    on_failure: true
    on_success: false              # no email on success — only failures


# ── Pipeline 3: Manual trigger (no schedule) ────────────────────────────────
# "Some pipelines are triggered by other DAGs or manually — schedule=null"
adhoc_reprocess:
  description: "Manual reprocessing for specific dates"
  schedule: null                   # no schedule — triggered manually
  owner: "data-engineering"
  tags: ["adhoc", "reprocess"]

  source:
    type: "s3"
    bucket: "insurance-raw"
    key_pattern: "claims/{{ ds }}/claims.json"
    conn_id: "aws_default"

  processing:
    type: "spark"
    script: "process_claims.py"
    spark_conf:
      spark.executor.memory: "8g"
      spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "400"

  destination:
    type: "postgres"
    conn_id: "postgres_prod"
    table: "claims_processed"

  quality_checks:
    min_records: 1
    max_file_size_mb: 10000
    check_output_exists: true

  notifications:
    email: ["data-engineering@company.com"]
    on_failure: true
    on_success: true

cards.title: Q1 Data Lakehouse Architecture
cards.prompt: Which two statements provide an explanation of data lakehouse architecture and its benefits?
cards.answer:
**Answers:**
- Lakehouse builds a data management and formatting layer on top of an open data lake
- Provides a unified platform for all data types with support for both BI and AI workloads

cards.title: Q2 Benefits Provided by Databricks
cards.prompt: Which three benefits are provided directly by Databricks?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "It provides scalable and redundant cloud-based data storage"

**Why wrong:** Databricks does NOT provide cloud storage. Storage is the cloud provider's responsibility (S3, ADLS, GCS). Databricks sits on top of it.

**Correct answers:**
- Available on and across multiple cloud platforms
- Unified security and governance approach to all data assets
- *(Third option: look for collaborative workspace or unified analytics platform)*

cards.title: Q3 Data Security and Governance
cards.prompt: How does Databricks support data security and governance across different cloud platforms?
cards.answer:
**Answer:** Databricks leverages **Unity Catalog** to provide a unified governance layer for all data and AI assets.

> **Note:** Correct spelling is **Unity Catalog**, not "Unit Catalog."

cards.title: Q4 AI Integration Benefits
cards.prompt: What two options describe benefits of integrating AI into the core of the Databricks platform?
cards.answer:
**Answers:**
- AI helps understand data structure, usage, and meaning — boosts productivity and optimizes workloads
- AI enhances user experience with always-ready assistant for debugging and code enhancements

cards.title: Q5 Unity Catalog Governance
cards.prompt: Unity Catalog benefits?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Unity Catalog provides a single interface to manage platform-wide permissions, audits, and data sharing for all data and AI governance needs.

cards.title: Q6 Databricks Notebooks
cards.prompt: What is the primary function of Databricks Notebooks?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Collaborative, reproducible environment for data practitioners with support for multiple languages.

cards.title: Q7 Natural Language for Non-Technical Users
cards.prompt: How does Databricks support non-technical users in gaining insights from data using natural language?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Through **AI/BI Genie Spaces** and **Databricks Assistant**, which allow users to interact with data using natural language prompts.

cards.title: Q8 Databricks Marketplace
cards.prompt: What is the core purpose of Databricks Marketplace?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "To provide a shared data storage solution for collaboration between partners and vendors"

**Why wrong:** Marketplace is NOT storage. It's a discovery and sharing platform.

**Correct answer:** To discover, share, and exchange data products, datasets, notebooks, ML models, and solutions from third-party providers.

cards.title: Q9 Lakeflow Jobs
cards.prompt: What is the role of Databricks Lakeflow Jobs?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Orchestrate all types of jobs within the platform, providing control flows, triggers, and monitoring.

cards.title: Q10 Data Warehousing on Databricks
cards.prompt: Which service supports data warehousing capabilities on Databricks?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "Lakehouse Foundation"

**Why wrong:** Lakehouse Foundation is the broader architecture layer, not the warehousing capability itself.

**Correct answer:** **Databricks SQL** (SQL Warehouses).

cards.title: Q11 Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines Features
cards.prompt: What are three main features of Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "Data visualization tooling"

**Why wrong:** Visualization is a BI/dashboard feature, not a pipeline feature.

**Correct answers:**
- Declarative ETL framework
- Unified batch and streaming support
- *(Third: automated data quality/expectations or automatic lineage tracking)*

cards.title: Q12 Databricks Mission
cards.prompt: What is the mission of Databricks?
cards.answer: **Answer:** To democratize data and AI.

cards.title: Q13 Beyond Data Lakehouse
cards.prompt: What problem does the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform solve beyond the data lakehouse?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Adds unified governance layer and AI-powered understanding of business context on top of lakehouse foundation, enabling agents that know your business.

cards.title: Q14 Lakebase Key Features
cards.prompt: What are three key features of Lakebase on Databricks?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong picks:**
- "Built on close-source storage format with fixed provisioned capacity" — **Wrong.** Lakebase uses **open formats** (Delta Lake)
- "Proprietary database engine exclusively for batch analytics" — **Wrong.** Supports transactional/operational workloads too

**Correct answer kept:** Separate compute and storage with pay-only-for-what-you-use pricing

**Correct answers for the other two:** Look for "built on open formats" and "supports transactional/operational workloads" or "fully managed with automatic scaling."

cards.title: Q15 Delta Sharing
cards.prompt: What is Delta Sharing, and its primary benefit?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Open, cross-platform sharing tool that allows sharing data without duplication.

cards.title: Q16 Databricks Assistant Purpose
cards.prompt: What is the purpose of Databricks Assistant?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "To monitor overall costs of the platform divided across multiple teams"

**Why wrong:** Cost monitoring is a different feature. Assistant is an AI coding helper.

**Correct answer:** An AI-powered assistant that helps users write, debug, and optimize code and queries.

cards.title: Q17 AI/BI Genie
cards.prompt: What capability does AI/BI Genie provide?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Allows users to ask natural language questions about their data, explore beyond pre-built dashboards, and maintain context between sessions.

cards.title: Q18 Unity Catalog — Universal Catalog
cards.prompt: What does it mean that Unity Catalog is the industry's only universal catalog?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Works across any engine, any client, any asset type, and any format, including open source support and Iceberg REST Catalog API.

cards.title: Q19 Open Data Formats Benefits
cards.prompt: What are two key benefits of using open data formats in a lakehouse architecture?
cards.answer:
**Your wrong pick:** "They guarantee faster query performance than any proprietary format"

**Why wrong:** Open formats do NOT guarantee faster performance. The benefit is flexibility and avoiding vendor lock-in.

**Correct answers:**
- Reduce unnecessary cost from maintaining multiple copies of data across platforms
- Prevent vendor lock-in and enable interoperability across tools and platforms

cards.title: Q20 Databricks Workspace Features
cards.prompt: Which three features are available within the Databricks Workspace?
cards.answer:
**Answers:**
- Lakeflow Jobs
- Catalog Explorer
- Notebooks

---

## Test 2: Lakeflow Jobs (70/100)

cards.title: Q1 Dashboard Tasks in Lakeflow Jobs
cards.prompt: When using dashboard tasks in Lakeflow Jobs, what is required for the dashboard to function properly?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| Must use only real-time data sources | ❌ |
| Must be private to the job creator | ❌ |
| **Must be published and connected to a SQL warehouse** | **✅** |
| Must be created using Python notebooks only | ❌ |

**Key concept:** Dashboards must be **published** and **connected to a SQL warehouse** to be used as job tasks.

cards.title: Q2 Notifications in Lakeflow Jobs
cards.prompt: Notifications can be triggered in which scenarios?
cards.answer: **Answer:** When the task begins, completes, or fails.

cards.title: Q3 File Arrival Triggers
cards.prompt: File Arrival Triggers are ideal for what type of data ingestion pattern?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Unpredictable or irregular data ingestion.

cards.title: Q4 SQL Query File Requirement
cards.prompt: What is required before using a SQL query file in a Lakeflow Job task?
cards.answer: **Answer:** The query file must be saved in the workspace.

cards.title: Q5 Minimum Job Structure
cards.prompt: What is the minimum structure required for a valid job?
cards.answer: **Answer:** A single task that defines the work to execute.

cards.title: Q6 Fan-Out Pattern
cards.prompt: How do downstream tasks execute in a fan-out pattern?
cards.answer: **Answer:** They run in parallel after the source task completes, each depending on the same upstream task.

cards.title: Q7 For Each Task
cards.prompt: What is the fundamental purpose of a For Each task?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Executing the same nested task multiple times per item in an input array.

cards.title: Q8 Continuous vs Scheduled Execution
cards.prompt: Which component is unique to the Continuous Trigger setup?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| Manual run options | ❌ |
| Cron expression setting | ❌ (this is for scheduled) |
| **Trigger status activation** | **✅** |
| Built-in retry management | ❌ |

**Key concept:** Continuous triggers have an **activate/pause toggle** (trigger status). Cron expressions are for scheduled triggers.

cards.title: Q9 Job-Level Parameters
cards.prompt: Where to specify a parameter value that applies to all tasks by default?
cards.answer: **Answer:** In the job-level "Job parameters" section when configuring the job.

cards.title: Q10 Main Purpose of Lakeflow Jobs
cards.prompt: What is the main purpose of Lakeflow Jobs?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Orchestrating and automating end-to-end data, analytics, and AI workflows.

cards.title: Q11 Compute Option for Scheduled Production
cards.prompt: Which compute option best fits: scheduled, no always-on cluster, auto shutdown after job?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| SQL Endpoint | ❌ |
| Interactive Clusters | ❌ |
| All-Purpose Cluster | ❌ (stays running, higher cost) |
| **Job Clusters** | **✅** |

**Key concept:** **Job Clusters** are created when job starts and **automatically terminate** when job completes. Cost-effective for scheduled production workloads.

cards.title: Q12 Unified Data Engineering Components
cards.prompt: Which three components constitute unified data engineering in Databricks Lakeflow?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| Jobs, MLflow, and Data Warehousing | ❌ |
| Connect, Storage, and Governance | ❌ |
| **Connect, Declarative Pipelines, and Jobs** | **✅** |
| Unity Catalog, Connect, and Processing Engine | ❌ |

**Key concept:** Lakeflow = three pillars:
- **Lakeflow Connect** — data ingestion
- **Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines** — ETL/transformation
- **Lakeflow Jobs** — orchestration

cards.title: Q13 Job Clusters vs Serverless Drawback
cards.prompt: What major drawback do job clusters have compared to serverless?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| Higher operational cost | ❌ |
| Limited data governance | ❌ |
| **Start-up time** | **✅** |
| Lack of Python support | ❌ |

**Key concept:** Job clusters need time to spin up VMs. **Serverless** clusters start near-instantly because compute is pre-provisioned by Databricks.

cards.title: Q14 Publish Task Dependencies
cards.prompt: How should the publish task be configured when it must run only if both validation tasks succeed?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Set the publish task to run if all dependencies succeed.

cards.title: Q15 If/Else Task
cards.prompt: How does the dynamic nature of the If/Else task enhance job pipelines?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Makes the workflow adaptable and responsive to actual results.

cards.title: Q16 Repair Run Behavior
cards.prompt: When initiating a repair run for a failed task, which tasks are rerun?
cards.answer: **Answer:** The failed task and all its dependent downstream tasks.

cards.title: Q17 Branching and Looping Capability
cards.prompt: Which Lakeflow Jobs capability supports branching to different tasks based on success/failure and loop-based execution?
cards.answer:
**Answer:** Task orchestration logic, including conditional and iterative tasks.

> **Note:** This answer appears correct conceptually. Review the exact wording of options in the test — may have been a close-call between similar options.

cards.title: Q18 Jobs and Tasks Relationship
cards.prompt: How do Jobs and Tasks relate?
cards.answer: **Answer:** A task defines an individual unit of work, while a job orchestrates and manages the execution of one or more tasks.

cards.title: Q19 Serverless Performance Optimized
cards.prompt: Best action for business-critical job that must start quickly and minimize execution time?
cards.answer: **Answer:** Enable Performance Optimized mode for the serverless job.

cards.title: Q20 Parameter for Orchestration Logic
cards.prompt: What parameter setting supports advanced orchestration logic like looping or conditional execution for a specific unit of work?
cards.answer:
| Option | Correct? |
|--------|----------|
| Job Parameters | ❌ (job-wide, not task-specific) |
| Global Environment Variables | ❌ |
| Notification settings | ❌ |
| **Task Parameters** | **✅** |

**Key concept:** **Task Parameters** are scoped to individual tasks. For orchestration logic (loops, conditionals) on a specific unit of work, task-level parameters give you per-task control.
